title: Greening cities to ensure biosphere functional integrity: Insights from Rotterdam and Lagos
authors: Joyeeta Gupta, Agni Kalfagianni, Chukwumerije Okereke, Fran Meissner, Abhigyan Singh, Carissa Champlin, Alyssa Delarosa, Sofi Joaquín Fernández, Miguel Avides, Zoé Sarolta Héjja, Chukwueloka Okeke, Elin Wahlqvist, Paola Fezzigna

title: To Be a Mental Disorder: Revisiting Behavioral Addictions
authors: Joshua B. Grubbs, Beáta Bőthe, Andrew (Hyounsoo) Kim, Nicholas Borgogna, Rory A. Pfund, Shane W Kraus
abstract: Behavioral addictions have been recognized in various forms for centuries, yet only three—Gambling Disorder, Gaming Disorder, and Compulsive Sexual Behavior Disorder—are currently included in formal diagnostic systems. In the past decade, research on these conditions has expanded dramatically in both volume and methodological rigor, drawing on longitudinal, neurobiological, and cross-cultural designs and evolving into a truly global science. Even so, the field remains beset by unresolved controversies. Chief among these is a persistent tendency to import substance use disorder concepts—tolerance, withdrawal, and dependence—that lack conceptual and empirical support when applied to behavior. Related challenges concern the over-pathologizing of normal engagement and a reliance on confirmatory, self-report measurement of uncertain validity. We argue that advancing the field requires sustained funding, theory grounded in the disorders themselves, objective and intensive-longitudinal methods, greater diversity, and public health and regulatory attention to increasingly technological environments.

title: Development and Preliminary Psychometric Evaluation of the STIGD-40: A Parent-Report Screening Tool for Internet Gaming Disorder in Children Aged 6–12 Years
abstract: Background: Internet Gaming Disorder (IGD) has received increasing clinical and research attention, but assessment tools specifically designed for younger children and based on parent-observable behavior remain limited. The Screening Tool for Internet Gaming Disorder in Children (STIGD-40) was developed as a parent-report measure of gaming-related difficulties in children aged 6–12 years. Method: An initial pool of 90 items was developed and refined through expert review, content-validity assessment, and item-level evaluation. A pilot dataset from 40 children aged 6–12 years was examined; 38 participants provided complete responses for the primary psychometric analyses. Internal consistency, corrected item–total correlations, exploratory factor analysis (EFA), and a preliminary confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) were examined. Results: The 40-item STIGD-40 demonstrated high internal consistency (Cronbach's α = .976; McDonald's ωt = .976), with corrected item–total correlations ranging from .489 to .876. Domain-level internal consistency coefficients ranged from .711 to .912. Exploratory factor analysis indicated substantial common variance, with two- and three-factor solutions accounting for 60.9% and 66.4% of the variance, respectively. The three-factor solution showed cross-loadings and did not correspond cleanly to the theoretically proposed nine-domain structure. Preliminary CFA of the nine-domain model produced unstable estimates and was therefore not interpreted as evidence of a confirmed factor structure. Conclusions: The STIGD-40 demonstrates promising preliminary internal consistency and item-level performance in this feasibility sample. However, the findings should be considered preliminary because of the small convenience sample and limitations in the factor analyses. The instrument should not currently be considered a validated diagnostic or screening measure, and no diagnostic cut-off is proposed. Larger studies using independent samples are needed to examine factor structure, construct validity, criterion validity, test–retest reliability, diagnostic accuracy, and clinically useful cut-off scores.

title: OVERLOOKED BEHAVIORAL ADDICTION: FORTUNE TELLING ADDICTION
abstract: Can fortune-telling be considered an addiction? To answer this question, this study explored parallels with behavioral addictions and analyzed a case report, identifying clear indicators of addiction. A survey was conducted using questionnaires about past childhood trauma, socio-demographic characteristics, and the presence of peer pressure to further investigate this assumption. Additionally, the study suggests further research paths for understanding the phenomenon of fortune-telling addiction and proposes potential preventive treatments. References were sourced from digital libraries, with all copyright respected and used appropriately. Keywords: fortune-telling addiction, behavioral addictions, impulse control disorders, addiction.

title: Stress and Substance Addiction Among College Students: Understanding the Psychological Triggers
abstract: Substance addiction among college students has emerged as a major public health concern closely associated with rising academic pressure, anxiety and stress. The transitional phase of college life exposes students to numerous physical, psychological and social challenges, which often drive them towards addictive substances as coping mechanisms. This paper aims to understand the psychological triggers linking stress to substance addiction among college students using secondary data from research articles, WHO , CDC reports and mental health studies. This review highlights that emotional instability, peer pressure, poor coping skills, and performance anxiety are key contributors to addiction vulnerability. Findings suggest that stress- induced addictions not only impairs academic performance but also leads to mental health complications such as depression and social withdrawal. The paper concludes that early mental health interventions, stress management programs, and awareness initiatives within college campuses and significantly reduce addiction tendencies among youth. Keywords: Stress, Addiction, College Students, Mental Health, Substance Abuse, Coping Mechanisms, Academic Pressure.

title: The Hidden Burden: Psychological Distress in Males with Substance Use Challenges
abstract: This study explores the nuanced relationship between internalized societal judgment and the experience of psychological distress among men facing substance use issues. It examines how perceived stigma contributes to emotional difficulties, specifically focusing on the interplay of anxiety, depressive symptoms, and stress. The research utilizes quantitative methods to assess these connections, highlighting the importance of addressing the psychological burden associated with substance use in male populations to improve mental health outcomes.

title: Exploring the Intersection of Language and Literacy in a Young Person with Autism, Learning Disability and Minimal Speech.
abstract: It is argued that language and literacy are inseparable for users of alternative and augmentative communication, and that literacy can offer a route to the acquisition of fully functioning language for non-verbal individuals with autistic spectrum disorder. This applied linguistics project explores the intersection of language and literacy in a young person with autism, learning disability and minimal speech. By use of multimodal conversation analysis, it reveals the range of everyday literacy practices used by the young person and how these literacy practices are drawn upon to make meaning in interaction. It finds that literacy practices constitute a significant part of their multimodal communicative repertoire and offer affordances as a mode of communication that breaks the limitations posed by their disabilities and the forms of AAC available to them.

title: MAGA Republicans as “Particularistic Authoritarians” on the Welfare State: Parallels with the European Populist Right
authors: Jake Haselswerdt, Hang Qi, Suhyun Cho
abstract: Has MAGA remade the Republican politics of the welfare state? While Republican voters have traditionally favored retrenchment, the so-called “populism” of the MAGA movement suggests that the social policy preferences of right-leaning Americans are due for reexamination. Drawing from the “particularistic authoritarian model” of European populist radical-right voters, we expect MAGA Republicans to favor benefits for deserving groups, stronger “workfare” policies, less social investment, and more restrictive deservingness criteria. We test these expectations using a 1,000-respondent module of the 2025 Cooperative Election Study. Factor analysis and regressions show that MAGA Republicans are substantially more supportive than non-MAGA Republicans of policies benefiting seniors and express levels of support comparable to those of Democrats and other respondents. MAGA Republicans also show somewhat stronger endorsement of restrictive deservingness criteria than other Republicans, while differences between the two Republican groups are less pronounced for social investment. Overall, the results indicate that MAGA Republicans do not simply favor either welfare state expansion or retrenchment. Instead, they distinguish among forms of social protection according to their beneficiaries and perceived deservingness.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Agriculture: Enhancing Yield and Sustainable Farming Practices among Farmers in India
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being applied across sectors, including agriculture. In India, agriculture remains central to employment, rural livelihoods, and national food security. Rising population pressure, climate change, declining land availability, pest and disease risks, labour shortages, and resource constraints have intensified the need for more productive and sustainable farming systems. This paper uses secondary data to examine how AI can enhance agricultural yield and support sustainable farming practices among farmers in India. It reviews applications such as precision agriculture, drones, crop disease detection, digital advisory services, market information systems, and resource optimisation tools. The paper also analyses the major barriers to AI adoption, including weak rural connectivity, high initial investment, limited digital literacy, and the need for localised solutions. The study concludes that AI has strong potential to improve productivity and sustainability in Indian agriculture, provided that adoption is supported through public investment, affordable access models, local-language advisory systems, farmer training, and public- private partnerships.

title: Are the children of homeowners increasingly advantaged? Trends in relative and absolute mobility of homeownership in Europe
authors: Selçuk Bedük, Enrico Benassi, Philipp M. Lersch
abstract: Homeownership is declining among younger generations across Europe. A common assumption is that this decline has been increasingly stratified by parental homeownership, due to rising house prices and the growing importance of parental financial support. We show that this assumption does not hold for the average European (and for most countries). Using data from EU-SILC 2011 and 2019 covering 24 European countries, we examine trends in relative and absolute mobility of homeownership for birth cohorts 1951 to 1984. On average, relative mobility remained largely stable across cohorts, while absolute mobility increased. The apparent stability of relative mobility masks a deeper structural cohort shift: downward mobility increased from 14 per cent to 38 per cent, while upward mobility declined from 23 per cent to 8 per cent between cohorts born in the early 1950s and early 1980s. Therefore, homeownership has declined significantly for both children of homeowners and renters. We also compare absolute and relative mobility trends across countries and show that they often diverge for two reasons. First, a mechanical effect of the origin distribution: in countries with widespread parental homeownership, relative mobility largely reflects changes in upward mobility. Second, the source of mobility: using two novel counterfactual simulations, we show that observed absolute mobility changes mainly stem from structural shifts in homeownership chances, rather than strengthening parent-child associations.

title: The Space Headright System: A Diachronic Analysis of First-Mover Elite Formation Mechanisms from Colonial Virginia to Twenty-First-Century Space Resource Law
abstract: This study examines how first-mover advantage was converted into durable elite dominance in seventeenth-century colonial Virginia, using this structural logic to critically evaluate twenty-first-century space resource law. Drawing on a Multilayered Frontier Capital Accumulation Model (MFCAM) that integrates frontier theory, world-systems theory, and institutional path dependence, the study addresses four research questions (RQ1–RQ4). Historical analysis shows how the First Families of Virginia (FFV), preempting land under the 1618 headright system, monopolized power through mutually reinforcing mechanisms of institutional pre-emption, marital closure, and symbolic capital accumulation, thereby converting land capital into political and cultural capital to maintain that dominance. At the same time, the study traces the formation of a lower-white stratum through indentured servitude, post-release landlessness, and racial divide-and-rule policies after Bacon's Rebellion (1676) and shows that elite and lower-class formation were two sides of the same institutional design. A comparison with the Massachusetts Bay Colony suggests these outcomes depended on early institutional choices. Based on these findings, the study conceptualizes a "Space Headright System" (SHS) comprising priority access to institutional design, revolving-door relations between regulators and industry, and the accumulation of legal precedent. By examining Section 402 of the 2015 U.S. Commercial Space Launch Competitiveness Act, the Artemis Accords, and national space resource laws, it assesses risks of lower-class formation such as space indentured servitude and space company towns. The study advances a conditional warning: if current legal trajectories continue, they suggest convergence toward a Virginia-type stratified order. To avert this, three policy recommendations (primary rules)—an international space cadastre, a Space Commons Fund, and treaty-based protections for later settlers—are proposed, alongside secondary design requirements to guard the implementing institutions against regulatory capture.

title: “I wouldn’t trust her with my life but...” - Exploring trust in voice-based assistants through user-generated content
abstract: Investigating trust in conversational AI, such as voice-based assistants (VBAs), is increasingly important for understanding their rising popularity and the tasks users entrust to them. Howev-er, since VBAs are technical devices perceived as human-like and sometimes serving as infor-mation sources, it is unclear what forms trust in them takes. Technical, interpersonal, and media trust approaches may all be relevant, yet previous studies have not fully considered this poten-tial multidimensionality of trust in AI, especially regarding the inclusion of media trust. Fur-thermore, research on VBAs lacks qualitative studies that provide insights into users’ perspec-tives. This study therefore pursues two objectives: First, to develop a more comprehensive theo-retical perspective on trust in VBAs by integrating technical, interpersonal, and media trust ap-proaches. Second, to empirically explore signs of trust in VBAs in German user-generated online content. To this end, we conducted a qualitative content analysis of 169 postings about Alexa, Siri, and Google Assistant found on marketplaces, under media coverage, and on dis-cussion platforms. The results show that users evaluate typical and new technical, interpersonal, and media trustworthiness indicators for VBAs and sometimes combine these dimensions when discussing AI capabilities. When explicitly speaking of trust, users mostly refer to the parent company in high-risk situations rather than to the VBA itself. Users also discuss aspects that may represent consequences, processes, and external factors of trust. Based on these findings, the paper proposes a preliminary model of hybrid trust in VBAs that can inform future research on trust in conversational AI.

title: A comment on “A Mother's Voice: Impacts of Spousal Communication Training on Child Health Investments”
abstract: Björkman Nyqvist et al. (2024) evaluate a randomized experiment in rural Uganda that studies whether strengthening women’s communication skills within marriage can shift household decisions toward greater investment in child health. All treatments provide health and nutrition training, varying whether mothers or fathers are involved, while one additional treatment incorporates a communication skills curriculum for mothers, allowing the authors to isolate the effect of communication. The authors report five core findings: First, women offered communication training report improved relationship quality. Second, the communication treatment increases the frequency of discussions between spouses about health and finances, but does not improve men’s health knowledge, indicating limited information transmission. Third, communication training does not increase the adoption of health-promoting behaviors beyond the gains from women’s health training alone. Fourth, the communication training shifts household spending, particularly on meat and fish. Fifth, none of the treatments improves the study's primary child health outcomes. We successfully computationally reproduce the paper's main claims, and show that the results are robust to corrections for multiple hypothesis testing, inclusion of control variables in analyses, and an alternative definition of relationship quality measure.

title: Recordable participation and the construction of student engagement in UK higher education
abstract: Student engagement is widely invoked as evidence of educational quality, yet its meanings are contested. This article examines how the concept is constructed and mobilised in UK higher education research, policy and institutional documentation. Drawing on Bacchi’s problematisation approach and Fairclough’s critical discourse analysis, it analyses a purposive corpus of 36 texts: 23 conceptual and research texts, two policy documents and 11 institutional documents from three West Midlands universities. Iterative close reading identifies three connected patterns. Multidimensional accounts of engagement are narrowed into visible proxies; evaluative infrastructures privilege meanings that can be documented and compared; and these constructions redistribute responsibility in ways that obscure unequal conditions of participation. Worked coding examples show how support, attendance, digital traces and regular logging become linked in institutional procedures. The article argues that recordable participation acquires authority because it can serve as evidence of both student conduct and institutional quality. This does not eliminate relational or participatory meanings, but places them at a disadvantage within systems organised around demonstrable performance. The contribution is to explain how the demand for evidence connects conceptual narrowing to unequal recognition, and why institutions should distinguish the visibility of participation from the conditions that make participation possible.

title: From Governance to Government? The European Commission and the three faces of politicisation
abstract: Research on the politicisation of the European Union has concentrated on reactive, bottom-up contestation of existing EU action. This article argues that such an understanding is incomplete because it conflates politicisation of issues with politicisation of institutions. We distinguish three faces of politicisation. Reactive politicisation refers to the public contestation of existing EU competences. Proactive politicisation occurs when supranational actors claim a political mandate in order to justify wider discretion. Induced politicisation emerges when intergovernmental conflict over already politicized state functions creates a vacuum that the Commission can try to fill, thereby inheriting the political character of the function itself. The empirical sections focus on induced politicisation. They reconstruct three episodes: Jean-Claude Juncker's attempt to use EMU deadlock to place the Commission at the centre of euro-area reform; the failed institutionalisation of an EU Finance Minister, a euro-area fiscal capacity, and a more political treasury function; and Ursula von der Leyen's attempts to centralise foreign-policy initiative during successive geopolitical crises. The argument is that politicisation does not only constrain supranational action. Under specific institutional conditions it can also widen supranational authority by transforming the Commission from guardian of the Treaties into a proto-governmental executive.

title: Sectoral Credit Reallocation and Consumer Credit Expansion: A Difference-in-Differences and Decomposition Analysis
abstract: This article examines sectoral bank-credit reallocation in Kyrgyzstan by combining a difference in differences (DiD) comparison around 2015 with a detailed accounting analysis for 2019–2025. The research question is how conclusions about reallocation depend on the comparison period, portfolio denominator and distinction between shares and real balances. Four focal lending categories are compared with a residual category in a historical series extended through 2025. The full-portfolio DiD contrast is +1.28 percentage points for 2010–2025, but −0.17 points when the window begins in 2012; the group gap already changes substantially before 2015. In the recent period, consumer loans rise from 11.8% to 33.6% of bank credit and account for 42.5% of the nominal increase in the outstanding portfolio. CPI-deflated non-consumer credit grows by 49.3%. Agriculture loses portfolio share while its real balance grows by 12.3%; industry and construction experience real declines of 34.7% and 17.5%. A symmetric decomposition separates the changing consumer-credit mix from redistribution within non-consumer lending. The integrated findings show why positive period-average sectoral contrasts can coexist with recent share losses and uneven real growth. DiD remains descriptive, and the decomposition is an accounting identity. Neither identifies the effect of accession or consumer-credit crowding out. Independent verification of the historical inputs remains incomplete.

title: A Middle Way proposal towards an equitable open access publishing model
abstract: Open access promised to widen participation in science, but the article-processing charge (APC) that funds much of gold open access has shifted the cost of publishing onto authors, reproducing rather than removing exclusion for the Global South. Writing as a journal editor based in Brazil, I argue that the instruments now relied upon, namely fee waivers, purchasing-power-parity pricing and transformative agreements, are each useful but insufficient, because each treats a structural problem as a matter of discounting. Latin America's non-commercial diamond model, exemplified by SciELO, has shown that affordable open access is achievable at roughly a tenth of the cost of a commercial APC, yet it remains constrained by limited global visibility. I propose a “Middle Way”: a public–private model in which national governments fund and own the core publishing infrastructure as a public good, as Brazil is now doing through the nationalisation of SciELO, while commercial firms are contracted, on transparent and unbundled terms, for the services they perform better, chiefly discoverability and global distribution. Ownership stays public, and the commercial sector becomes a contracted supplier rather than the owner of the venue. The proposal's scope condition is ownership: it fits systems where the publishing venue is, or can become, publicly or institutionally owned.

title: Youth physical activity in transitioning subsistence societies varies by biological maturity and market integration
authors: Lee Gettler, Vidrige Kandza, Jessica K. Hlay, Haneul Jang, Rahul C. Oka, Francy Kiabiya Ntamboudila, Derlan Brenez Bihoundou Mouketou, Chelvin Destin Siassia Vindou, Evrahd Ngalekandza, Brel Koubemba
abstract: Background: Physical activity patterns across childhood and adolescence help shape long-term health and contribute to the allocation of limited resources among growth, maintenance, and reproduction during maturation. The vast majority of data on youth physical activity comes from post/industrial societies. We know relatively little about youth physical activity in smaller-scale subsistence contexts where youth routinely contribute to production and household tasks under energetically demanding conditions. Methods: Using wearable technology, we measured moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA) and sedentary behavior among BaYaka forager and Bantu fisher-farmer youth (N=206; obs. days=798) in the Congo Basin. These communities live under energetically-demanding conditions and varying degrees of early market integration. Results: Youth were highly physically active, averaging 4.07 hours of daily MVPA. Forager females had the highest routine MVPA, although foragers were more sedentary than farmers. Developmentally, youth who were more pubertally advanced engaged in a lower percentage of daily MVPA, and older youth were more sedentary. Youth residing in the most market-integrated village engaged in a lower percentage of daily MVPA compared to the least-integrated village. Conclusions: Our findings suggest that youth facultatively adjust their activity levels as they biologically mature and that physical activity is lower with incipient market integration. The routinely high levels of youth physical activity in these communities underscore the gap between subsistence lifestyles in energetically-demanding environments and physical activity in post/industrialized societies. From a global public health perspective, our findings highlight a crucial window during early economic transitions for public health interventions aimed at preventing physical inactivity and the chronic disease burden associated with lifestyle shifts.

title: Between resistance and negotiation. Intellectual property as a survival strategy for media facing AI and digital platforms
authors: Javier Díaz-Noci, Javier Odriozola-Chéné, Rosa Pérez Arozamena, Koldobika Meso-Ayerdi, Simón Peña-Fernández
abstract: Introduction. Generative AI has intensified tensions between news organisations and technology platforms over intellectual property, audience traffic and journalism’s economic sustainability. The report examines how leading Spanish digital media have framed AI since ChatGPT’s emergence, while considering the subsequent disruption caused by Google AI Overviews and AI Mode. Methods. The study combines quantitative content analysis with legal and industry analysis. It examines 242 AI-related articles published between January 2022 and December 2024 by leading Spanish digital-native and legacy outlets, selected according to GfK DAM audience data. Frequency distributions and contingency tables assess thematic frames and editorial positions. Results. Intellectual property emerges as the central underlying conflict. Coverage concentrates on authorship (68%), ethics and legal liability (45%), business models and licensing (32%), and employment (21%). Legacy media generally frame AI as a threat to journalistic assets, whereas digital-native outlets emphasise efficiency and commercial opportunities. Civil society and journalists themselves remain marginal in the debate. Google’s AI-generated summaries further intensify concerns by retaining users within the platform and reducing referral traffic. Discussion. Intellectual property is becoming both a defensive right and a bargaining asset. The sector is consequently shifting from litigation towards licensing, collective negotiation and technological adaptation, although confidential agreements may strengthen major publishers while marginalising smaller outlets.

title: Insights into the scale, organisation, implementation and motivations behind dog culling in a rabies-endemic setting
authors: Tasmin Alexander, Kennedy Lushasi, Lwitiko Sikana, Anna Czupryna, Elaine Ferguson, Mirava Yuson, Deborah Nadal, Nicholas Hanley, Nai Rui Chng, Sarah Cleaveland
abstract: Culling is recognised as ineffective and potentially counterproductive for sustainable dog population management and rabies control, yet the practice persists in many countries. Empirical data on the scale, organisation, implementation and motivations behind culling remain sparse, limiting understanding of its persistence, and implications. Focusing on Tanzania, a rabies-endemic country where culling has been documented, this study uses a mixed-methods approach, combining two structured surveys (survey of occurrence, n = 51; survey of practice in districts reporting culling, n = 16) and in-depth interviews with district and field-based veterinary and livestock officers (n = 8). Culling was reported in 45% of surveyed districts (23/51). Culling events were reportedly led by veterinary departments, often with involvement of other sectors and communities, with officers also describing communities as carrying out some culling independently. Culling was motivated by complaints, requests and orders about the number of and harms attributed to free-roaming dogs. Roaming dogs were culled regardless of ownership, sterilisation and vaccination status, using methods inconsistent with humane killing standards. Extrapolating from the survey data, using a stochastic simulation, we estimate approximately 26,000 dogs (95% CI 20,000-33,000) are culled annually nationwide. Culling was difficult to reconcile with evidence-based international guidance on dog population management and rabies control, national animal welfare legislation, and One Health principles, underscoring the need to understand and address the factors sustaining it. Addressing culling will require engaging with the wider concerns motivating the practice, and with the sectors and communities involved.

title: Citizens’ Support for EU AI Sovereignty Policy
abstract: This article examines EU citizens’ support for EU policy to attain digital sovereignty regarding Artificial intelligence (AI). Promoting domestic industries in AI is crucially important for attaining AI sovereignty. Yet, AI sovereignty policy ultimately hinges on support by the European public, and protective policy intervening in the EU AI market may be felt directly – and negatively – by citizens. Using survey data from Lithuania, the Netherlands, Romania, and Sweden, we examine how much citizens support AI sovereignty policy even if this comes with costs and study how political and AI attitudes are associated with this trade-off evaluation. The analysis shows that EU-centrism is positively associated with support for AI sovereignty policy whereas positive attitudes toward AI and higher trust in US and Chinese tech companies show negative associations. The results have important consequences for the EU’s possibilities to garner public support for an AI sovereignty policy agenda.

title: Accountability Among Allies: Intra-Party Competition and the Electoral Cost of Scandal
authors: Stefano Sangiovanni, Giovanna Maria Invernizzi, Andrea Ceron
abstract: When do voters electorally punish politicians for scandals? We argue that a scandal changes votes only when it can tip voters who are near indifference between candidates, and that intra-party contests place far more voters in that position than inter-party contests. We formalize this argument in a model of electoral sanctioning and test it in a pre-registered conjoint experiment on 3,000 U.S. adults. The scandal penalty is about 57% larger in intra-party contests, and, as the model predicts, the amplification appears even when both candidates come from the party the voter opposes. Inter-party choice settings may therefore understate how strongly voters punish misconduct when credible co-partisan alternatives are available.

title: Industrializing Eastern Slovakia and Its Post- Socialist Legacy: The Cases of the East Slovak Ironworks in Košice and the Metal Working Factory in Medzev
abstract: This article explores patterns of post-socialist reindustrialization in Eastern Slovakia—a region deeply shaped by heavy socialist industrialization and subsequently exposed to the tumultuous “manager’s privatization” of the 1990s. Bridging social and economic history, it argues that inherited industrial legacies—in know-how, infrastructure, workforce, and export orientation— persisted even after a sharp decline in the first decade following the fall of socialism. Through two case studies—the “giant” East Slovak Ironworks near the regional capital Košice and a smaller metalworking factory in the nearby town of Medzev—the article shows how foreign investment, limited state intervention, and local agency jointly enabled the partial revitalization of regionally significant industries, despite the absence of a coherent industrial policy and the dismantling of state coordination after 1989. Drawing on archival records, contemporary press, and biographical interviews, the study traces the long-term trajectories of these sites within both socialist development agendas and post-socialist restructuring. By demonstrating how industrial continuity and reactivation emerged largely in the absence of strategic governance and industrial policy, the article contributes to broader debates on post-socialist varieties of capitalism, state capacity, and the uneven geography of industrial transformation. By foregrounding continuity and reinvention, this nuanced perspective challenges binary accounts of post-socialist change.

title: Digital Civic Activism and Configurations of Social-Identity Factors: Protest Campaigns in Gaming Communities on Reddit
abstract: This study examines the conditions associated with successful digital protest campaigns in online video-game consumer communities. The theoretical framework combines the Social Identity Model of Collective Action (SIMCA) with research on digital political consumerism. The analysis covers 20 campaigns coordinated on Reddit between 2019 and 2024 and includes five conditions: discursive indicators of collective efficacy (EFFIC), group identification (IDENT), and group-based anger (ANGER), as well as the share of new/low-karma accounts (ANON) and the concentration of activity among the most active participants (LEAD). The empirical corpus contains 312,816 comments; an additional 8,055 comments were manually coded for validation and comparison with automated annotation. Fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA) is used to identify configurations associated with outcomes. None of the five conditions is necessary for a concession by the campaign target. The parsimonious solution contains three alternative configurations, but the most robust result is the combination of high group-based anger and low concentration of activity among the most active participants (ANGER × ~LEAD). This path survives most sensitivity checks and indicates that concessions in this sample are associated with mass, emotionally salient, and relatively decentralized mobilization. At the same time, cases of intense mobilization without concessions show that community-level characteristics are insufficient to explain outcomes without considering the cost of concession, the type of demand, and the position of the target organization. Artificial-intelligence tools were used in the research process and in preparing this manuscript. A pretrained CardiffNLP model was used for emotion classification; Gemini was used for automated EFFIC and IDENT annotation; Claude models assisted with the development and checking of replication code; and ChatGPT was used to translate the manuscript. The research question, case selection, operationalization, calibration decisions, result validation, and substantive interpretation were performed by the researcher.

title: From Berberism to Kabyle-Nationalism. Historical Analysis of Berberism in Algeria between 1930 and 2005.
abstract: This article examines the historical development of Berberism in Algeria from the emergence of Algerian nationalist movements in the 1930s to the aftermath of the Black Spring of 2001. It argues that Berberism should not be understood as a stable political ideology with a fixed substantive meaning, but rather as a changing political practice through which the idea of a distinctive Berber identity has been mobilised in response to particular political contexts. The analysis distinguishes three phases in the development of Berber activism. The first, exemplified by the Berber Crisis of 1948–49, was largely an elite struggle within the Algerian nationalist movement over the definition of the Algerian nation and the recognition of its linguistic and cultural plurality. The second, crystallised in the Berber Spring of 1980, transformed Berberism into a broader social movement centred on cultural recognition, linguistic rights and opposition to state Arabisation. During the subsequent period of political liberalisation and civil war, Berber activism became increasingly institutionalised through political parties, social movements and transnational networks. The third phase, associated with the Black Spring of 2001, marked a significant reorientation. The declining legitimacy of established Berberist parties and the emergence of the Citizens’ Movement shifted political mobilisation toward territorial, socio-economic and increasingly Kabylia-centred claims. Drawing on concepts of political identity, recognition, nationalism and imagined communities, the article argues that this development contributed to the emergence of a specifically Kabyle nationalism. Whereas Berberism provided a broader cultural and transnational identity, it lacked a clearly defined territorial project capable of consolidating a common political community. The post-2001 mobilisation in Kabylia, by contrast, increasingly linked cultural identity to a specific homeland, territorial political structures and demands for autonomy. The article therefore conceptualises the transition from Berberism to Kabyle nationalism not as a linear transformation, but as a reconfiguration of political actors, strategies, territorial imaginaries and claims to collective self-determination. The article was written in 2012.

title: Closure without Resolution in European Prison Oversight
abstract: Compliance with judgments of the European Court of Human Rights is conventionally recorded as a terminal status: a case is open or closed, a judgment executed or pending, an obligation met or unmet. These measures enable scholarly comparison, but they cannot show how a state engages with the supervision of a judgment or whether reform of prison conditions endures. As such, this article treats compliance as conduct and asks whether the closure of supervision reflects durable improvement in the conditions a judgment addressed. Drawing on the documentary record of Committee of Ministers supervision in three pilot-judgment jurisdictions (i.e., Italy, Romania, and Hungary), with two contextual comparators (i.e., Spain and England and Wales), it codes state disclosures for opacity and stance and reconstructs responsiveness descriptively from the dated supervisory sequence. Two independent coders reached strong agreement (Krippendorff’s alpha of 0.88 for stance and 0.90 for opacity, on small, well-specified eligible data sets). The cases did not form a single compliance scale but displayed distinct configurations. Specifically, Italy was transparent but shifted in its stated position before closure in 2016; Romania combined continuing engagement with capacity explanations; and Hungary combined formal but insubstantial engagement with selective disclosure. Set against current prison occupancy, the state that had completed supervision was the most overcrowded: Italy recorded 120.7 occupants per 100 places, exceeding Hungary's 114.5 and Romania's 111.2. Because the occupancy snapshot postdated Italy's closure, it could not reveal whether closure caused the later overcrowding, but it did manifest that closure did not secure lasting improvement in reforms. The article frames this durability gap as a problem of means-ends decoupling and offers a reproducible method for distinguishing compliance conduct from the substantive conditions oversight exists to change.

title: Beyond Good and Bad Controls: Endogenous Legal Factors in Sentencing Research
abstract: Observational studies of institutional decision-making often rely on explanatory variables that are themselves partly constructed through the process under investigation. In sentencing research, many legal factors are defined by the judge and may therefore act simultaneously as confounders and mediators. Controlling for them may introduce post-treatment bias, whereas omitting them may reintroduce confounding bias. We propose overcoming this impasse by conceptualising judicially-defined legal factors as variables affected by measurement error. Using a typical regression model of racial disparities in the U.S. Federal Courts, we demonstrate how sensitivity analyses based on SIMEX and Monte Carlo simulations can be used to assess the bias arising from judicial disagreement and judicial prejudice. We show that even modest levels of uncertainty in discretionary legal factors can generate substantial and unpredictable bias, affecting estimates of racial disparities even when measurement error is entirely random and therefore unrelated to race.

title: The Self-Destruction Hypothesis of Consumerism: The Inflation of Consumption Standards and the Mismatch with Household Income
abstract: This paper proposes and develops a theoretical proposition concerning the endogenous evolution of consumerism: consumerism may not necessarily come to an end because of “excessive consumption”; rather, by continuously raising the consumption standards associated with “normal life,” it may make an increasing number of ordinary workers unable to participate in the consumption patterns it has itself constructed, thereby eroding the demand base on which it depends. Consumer demand has a positive expansionary effect during the early stages of economic development. The paper then explains why social consumption standards may continue to rise through three channels: firm competition; positional goods and social comparison; and the diffusion and amplification of cultural products and social media. On this basis, it argues that under conditions of market competition, firms simultaneously need to expand effective demand on the consumer side and have an inherent incentive to control labor costs, creating a structural mismatch between the growth of workers’ incomes and the rise of consumption standards. When consumption standards grow persistently faster than the actual disposable incomes of ordinary workers, consumption behavior may shift from “keeping up with the standard” toward “reducing, postponing, or even exiting consumption,” with particularly concentrated effects in marriage and family formation. Using the decline in China’s marriage and birth rates, the rising consumption standards associated with wedding photography and housing, and the adjustment of the real-estate sector as illustrative empirical cases, the paper distinguishes two post-turning-point adjustment paths—“structural consumption downgrading” and “aggregate-demand-driven consumption contraction”—and discusses the possibilities and limits of external trade as a substitute for domestic demand. The paper further constructs a conceptual income–consumption-standard mismatch model to characterize the pressure generated by the divergence between income and consumption standards and its transmission to consumption behavior, family formation, and future demand. Finally, it proposes four policy directions: optimizing social-media algorithms, establishing a Departmental Employment Quality Index (DEQI) for higher education, reducing the minimum cost of basic living, and limited government intervention in consumption externalities.

title: Localized Multimodal Interfaces in English-Default Mobile Apps: A Multimodal Discourse Analysis of Non-Native Users' Perception
abstract: The purpose of this research project is to examine how English-default and localized multimodal mobile interfaces affect user perception across six constructs: comprehension, cognitive load, motivation, inclusivity, tonal reception, and credibility. Onboarding and upgrade screens from three globally used applications (Duolingo, Spotify, and Notion) were analyzed as experienced by Italian-locale users whose devices were set to Italian, but whose interfaces remained predominantly in English. A mixed-methods design was used, combining qualitative multimodal discourse analysis of 24 application screenshots with quantitative descriptive statistics from a Likert-scale perception survey (n = 56). The multimodal analysis utilized a visual grammar framework, whereas the survey constructs were based on cognitive load theory, Self-Determination Theory (SDT), and digital credibility research. Results show moderately positive comprehension and tonal reception across all three applications, largely supported by visual elements such as mascots, icons, and color-coded calls to action. Inclusivity scored lowest overall. Italian L1 participants reported higher perceived effort and lower credibility than non-Italian participants, with the sharpest differences observed in upgrade flows. The findings are examined in the context of linguistic justice, English as a lingua franca, and discursive legitimation. The findings support biphasic localization strategies and suggest avenues for future research employing behavioural metrics and expanded participant samples. Keywords: multimodal discourse analysis, localization, English-default interfaces, cognitive load, linguistic justice, user experience, mobile applications

title: Algorithms of Fabrication: Generative AI and the Reshaping of Democratic Resilience and Regime Stability
abstract: The 2024 election cycle marked a strategic turning point in digital influence. While previous interference relied on algorithmic distribution, Generative AI (GenAI) has introduced a paradigm of automated fabrication, fundamentally reshaping the mechanics of political stability. This article examines GenAI as a strategic amplifier whose impact is filtered through the institutional structures of four distinct regime types. In Strong Democracies, synthetic content accelerates epistemic erosion, dissolving the shared factual reality necessary for deliberation. In Weak Democracies, it fuels precision radicalization, enabling populist actors to bypass institutional gatekeepers and dismantle oversight from within. Conversely, Strong Autocracies co-opt GenAI for digital fortification and automated narrative control, while Weak Autocracies face synthetic volatility, where low-cost deepfakes bypass porous censorship, triggering rapid destabilization. The article concludes by proposing a four-pillar policy framework including standardized content provenance, liability reform, strategic hardware controls, and transnational enforcement to restore information integrity in an increasingly deregulated global environment.

title: How serotonin promotes sleep, cognitive flexibility and resilience, and lowers withdrawal and craving.
abstract: These theoretical findings introduce new circuit-based mechanisms HOW serotonin causes its antidepressant, anxiolytic, safety signaling, well-being, and anti-withdrawal effects, sleep, loss of awareness, awareness, learning, well-being, and resilience. They elucidate neural pathways through which both MRN and DRN inhibit lateral habenula (LHb), increase cognitive flexibility, calm inflammation and craving, lower oxidative stress, promote homeostasis, satisfaction, and feeling at ease. This work shows new findings HOW worries, stress and excitement mutually inhibit slow wave sleep promoting regions. HOW slow wave sleep (SWS) attenuates stress and craving, and HOW serotonin promotes cognitive flexibility, socializing and resilience to stress. Paper explains neural mechanisms underneath these effects by proposed neural interactions between the medial habenula, interpeduncular nucleus and median raphe, the MHb-IPN-MRN circuit that promotes SWS, and substances that induce or suppress it. This perspective proposes how ventral anterior cingulate cortex (vACC) signals safety and well-being, activates DRN, promotes safety, contentment, and calm stress and deprivation. It claims that overstimulated LHb (in fear, depression, anxiety, worries, trauma, pain) causes insomnia because it hinders MRN serotonin release. Main claim explains that stress overstimulates noradrenaline release that consequently mutually suppresses MHb, IPN, and MRN, including glutamate, GABA and serotonin release. Thus, the MHb-IPN-MRN activation mutually inhibits stress, anxiety and withdrawal, by inhibiting the LHb, LC noradrenaline release, and ventral tegmental area (VTA) dopamine and corticotropine releasing hormone (CRH) release.

title: Price elasticity of demand for cigarettes in Spain: A segment-specific analysis (2005–2025)
authors: Gema Aonso-Diego, Ángel García-Pérez, Andrea Krotter Díaz
abstract: Background. Increasing tobacco prices through taxation is widely recognized as the most cost-effective intervention for reducing consumption and the associated health burden. This study aims to estimate the price elasticity of demand for conventional cigarettes (by distinguishing between low-, medium-, and high-price brands) using official Spanish sales data from 2005 to 2025, controlling for tobacco-control regulations (Acts 28/2005 and 42/2010), the COVID-19 lockdown, underlying trends, wages, and dynamic effects. Methods. A log-linear demand model using monthly cigarette sales data in Spain was estimated to analyze the association between cigarette prices and consumption levels. Models included controls for tobacco control policies, wages, seasonality, long-term trends, dynamics, and COVID-19-related disruptions. In addition, segment-specific analyses were conducted by classifying cigarette brands into low-, medium-, and high-price segments. Results. Tobacco control legislation (particularly Act 42/2010) was associated with significant reductions in cigarette sales. The overall price elasticity of demand was −0.596, with marked heterogeneity across segments: high-price brands were more responsive (−0.91) than medium- (−0.214) and low-price brands (−0.225). Consumption was also influenced by external factors, including the COVID-19 pandemic and income fluctuations. Conclusions. Tobacco taxation is the most effective regulatory measure, with an overall elasticity (−0.596) exceeding those reported in previous studies. The high-price segment shows the greatest responsiveness, while the relative inelasticity in low- and medium-price brands suggests a need for policies that reduce price gaps to prevent down-trading. These findings should guide future regulations, integrating tax increases with cessation support to maximize the public health impact.

title: The Chemical Harness: Antipsychotic Drugs as Multi‑Generational Pollutants and the Hidden Burden of Reproductive Disruption
abstract: Antipsychotic medications occupy a unique and troubling nexus in modern medicine: they are simultaneously indispensable treatments for severe psychiatric illness, iatrogenic drivers of a dopamine‑supersensitivity cycle that renders patients pharmacologically dependent, and globally distributed environmental contaminants whose persistence, bioaccumulation, and reproductive toxicity are systematically underestimated. This review synthesises the chemical lineage of antipsychotics from the synthesis of chlorpromazine to third‑generation partial agonists; quantifies the expansion of their global market, now projected to exceed USD 32 billion by 2033; documents the extensive off‑label deployment of these agents in elderly populations despite black‑box warnings of excess mortality; and critically examines the under‑recognised burden of hyperprolactinaemia, sexual dysfunction, and impaired spermatogenesis. We place antipsychotics—together with their pharmacologically active metabolites—within the pantheon of recalcitrant environmental pollutants, arguing that they deserve regulatory scrutiny comparable to that accorded to PFAS and neonicotinoids. A cheminformatics analysis of 101 compounds highlights the structural similarity between parent drugs and their active metabolites, the isolation of the dioxin TCDD, and the coherent cluster formed by non‑halogenated β‑blockers, which offer a potential pathway toward greener pharmacology. We conclude that the historical origins of these agents as short‑term sedatives, the availability of less toxic alternatives, and the role of environmental and lifestyle factors in driving the very symptoms these drugs target call for a fundamental reassessment of the prescribing paradigm.

title: The PROTECT Protocol: A Framework for Integrating Brain Health into Overdose Response Systems
abstract: Canada's overdose crisis is most often measured in deaths. What remains largely unseen is the far larger population of people who survive. Between 2016 and 2025, more than 53,000 Canadians died from drug overdoses. Over the same period, an estimated 1.1 to 1.6 million non-fatal overdose events occurred, each one a potential brain injury caused by oxygen deprivation, disrupted blood flow, or the direct toxic effects of drugs on brain tissue. For many survivors, these are not isolated events. Repeated overdoses produce cumulative neurological harm that is often subtle, undiagnosed and untreated. The capacities most commonly affected, memory, judgment, impulse control and emotional regulation, are precisely those required for recovery, stability and safety. Conservative estimates suggest that hundreds of thousands of Canadians and likely more than one million, are living with some degree of overdose-related brain injury, most of it invisible to systems designed for acute emergency response rather than long-term cognitive care. Treating substance use disorder without recognizing cognitive impairment fundamentally limits what existing interventions can achieve. This is not a failure of effort or compassion. It is a misalignment between system design and neurological reality, one that this report is designed to address. The PROTECT Protocol is a learning health system framework, one in which care delivery and knowledge generation are integrated. The model responds to the gap that separates the generation of clinical evidence from its application in practice. PROTECT is designed to close that gap, and is organized around five pillars

title: Suppression, Dissociation, and Withdrawal: An Integrative Model of Addiction Maintenance
abstract: Current models of addiction fail to provide a unified explanation for three persistent anomalies: (1) relapse after years of sustained abstinence when no physiological dependence remains, (2) withdrawal symptoms in behavioral addictions where no exogenous chemical agent is involved, and (3) the efficacy of mutually contradictory therapeutic approaches, such as motivational interviewing, Alcoholics Anonymous, Addictive Voice Recognition Technique, Allen Carr's method, Internal Family Systems therapy, and mindfulness-based relapse prevention. The present paper proposes an integrative model in which the maintenance of addiction is driven not by the impulse to use, but by its suppression. Beginning from the well-established premises that chronic addiction is maintained by avoidance of a negative state rather than pursuit of reward (Koob and Volkow, 2010) and that ambivalence is its central psychological feature (Miller and Rollnick, 2013), the model demonstrates through proof by elimination that suppression is the only logically coherent resolution of genuine ambivalence in an acting agent. This suppression instantiates the willpower paradox (Goschke and Job, 2023)—the structural impossibility of a unified subject exerting control over itself—which is resolved by adopting their third proposed solution: the subject is not unified. The model identifies Wegner's (1994) ironic process as the mechanism of entry into this split: sustained suppression generates two parallel, opposed, informationally asymmetric lines of action—the same structural condition that Hilgard (1977) demonstrated produces functional dissociation in experimental settings. The resulting dissociative structure compensates for the irreconcilable conflict by preserving the addictive impulse as a functionally autonomous position, informationally isolated from the individual's values and decisions—producing what is experienced as “uncontrollable” behavior despite genuine efforts to stop. The model generates seven testable predictions and provides the first unified account of why diverse and seemingly incompatible therapeutic methods each target different links of the same underlying mechanism.

title: Neurobiological Modulation of Substance Use Without Neurotoxicity: A Conceptual Framework for Non-Damaging Inhibition of Addictive Behaviors
abstract: Substance use disorders represent a complex interaction between neurobiological, behavioral, and environmental factors. Current pharmacological approaches often focus on substitution or aversive mechanisms, frequently accompanied by undesirable neurological or systemic side effects. This conceptual study proposes a non-damaging neurobiological modulation strategy aimed at inhibiting substance use without inducing neurotoxicity or cognitive impairment. The framework integrates principles from neuroplasticity, reward circuit modulation, receptor-level interference, and behavioral conditioning, emphasizing selective pathway inhibition rather than global neurotransmission suppression. By targeting specific neural circuits involved in craving and reinforcement—while preserving executive and emotional functions—this approach seeks to reduce substance-seeking behavior without compromising brain integrity. This paper does not propose a finished pharmacological compound but outlines a biologically plausible and ethically grounded research direction. The model may serve as a foundation for future experimental studies in addiction neuroscience, pharmacology, and behavioral intervention development.

title: Single Family Schoolyards: Residential Zoning and School Segregation.
authors: Stan Oklobdzija, Nicholas Marantz, Carolina Reid
abstract: Though the Supreme Court's 1954 decision in Brown v. Board of Education outlawed explicit segregation of public schools, segregation has remained stubbornly persistent in the intervening decades. What explains continuous racial segregation in the absence of explicit policy? One possible driver is America's built environment--designed with similar segregationist impulses but not subject to the same corrective legal action. Zoning and land use policy influence where households of different means can live, thereby sorting their children across schools. We investigate this link drawing on housing unit counts from the American Community Survey, apportioned to 923 school district boundaries and 13,002 school attendance zones with 27 million residential parcels. We find that districts where single-family and multifamily housing is spread unevenly across attendance zones are more segregated by race and income. Schools with attendance zones that contain a higher proportion of single-family detached residences enroll a disproportionately high share of Asian and White students, as compared with their districts. When an attendance zone boundary is redrawn to encompass a higher share of single-family housing, its Asian and White share increases further. These findings help illuminate how land use policy influences educational segregation and contributes to literature on how policies that regulate the built environment affect racial sorting.

title: The shape of NSF openness to newcomers: same share, fewer doors
authors: Jingwen Zhang, Hengyi Fu, Haining Wang
abstract: Openness to new investigators is often judged by the share of awards to principal investigators (PIs) without recent funding. We examine it in fiscal year (FY) 2026, when the US National Science Foundation (NSF) made the fewest new grants in four decades. NSF made 30% fewer new research projects than in FY2025, and the number of funded PIs with no NSF award as PI in the previous decade (newcomers) fell nearly as much, yet their share of new projects barely moved (34.5% to 34.3%). CAREER, NSF's main early-career award, added 3.3 percentage points to the newcomer share, offsetting the closure of three early-career programs reserved for institutions outside the Carnegie R1 tier (−3.0 points). The stable share hid a narrowing of reach. Where those programs closed, newcomers fell by 13% at R1 universities and by 66% at institutions below R2, whereas in engineering, which kept its program, newcomers below R2 rose. CAREER's growth went to institutions with more prior NSF projects, and NSF's grant obligations to institutions below R2 fell by 44%, twice the fall at R1 universities, with no offset from other federal research agencies. Per dollar, the closed programs had produced more papers than CAREER or standard grants.

title: Platform visibility and protest recirculation in the Cockroach Janta Party movement
abstract: This paper examines how the Cockroach Janta Party connected digital communication and street protest in India between May and July 2026. I draw on nineteen public documentary records and a separate retrospective account of my participation. I follow calls to attend demonstrations, a request to share protest photographs and videos, Sonam Wangchuk's involvement, and disputes over platform access. In my early visits, I remember small gatherings, people who stayed only briefly, and volunteers who hoped the protest would grow but were unsure how far it would spread. These observations make it difficult to assume that online popularity leads to sustained participation. I use a visibility-action-recirculation framework to examine how gatherings produce material that returns to digital circulation. A limited comparison with Nepal's September 2025 protests considers how people maintain communication when services are restricted. The evidence documents deliberate organizing and reported interruptions. It does not establish how recommendation systems, emotional appeals or recirculated material affected attendance. Keywords: Cockroach Janta Party; platform visibility; digital protest; recirculation; platform governance; India; Nepal

title: Lexical, Syntactic, and Semantic Distances Across Five Languages: A Reproducible Framework Integrating Python NLP and R Statistical Modeling
abstract: Quantitative comparisons across languages have traditionally relied on manually curated typological features, while recent advances in multilingual language models provide new opportunities for large-scale cross-linguistic research. This paper presents a reproducible framework that integrates natural language processing and statistical modeling to examine lexical, syntactic, and semantic variation across English, Chinese, Spanish, French, and German. Drawing on a corpus of 1,860 Wikipedia articles, the study combines traditional linguistic indicators with LaBSE-based semantic representations. The results show that language differences dominate the observed variation, with Chinese forming a distinct outlier and English and Spanish exhibiting the greatest similarity. Moreover, lexical-syntactic distances are significantly correlated with semantic distances derived from Transformer embeddings. These findings suggest that traditional quantitative measures and modern representation-learning approaches capture complementary aspects of language structure and meaning. The framework offers a scalable methodology for multilingual corpus linguistics and quantitative typology.

authors: Stan Oklobdzija, Nicholas Marantz, Carolina Reid

title: Machine-Learning Geographic Sampling Frames Underrepresent People on the Move in Fragile Settings
authors: Andrea Carlomaria Caflisch, Daniel Masterson, Stephen Daniel O'Connell, Ettan Patel, Julia Smith Omomo
abstract: Political science research often studies difficult-to-locate populations: internally displaced persons (IDPs), returnees, migrants, and others who move during war, disaster, or crisis. We compare machine-learning (ML)-generated building footprints against high-resolution satellite imagery for constructing sampling frames. In displacement- affected communities in Iraq, 15.5% of ML points were invalid or duplicated, and manual additions constituted 19% of the final hybrid frame. Manual additions reached 10.2 percentage points more IDPs in rural communities and 10.1 more returnees in urban areas. We attribute differences to two mechanisms: temporary and informal shelters are harder for ML algorithms to detect, while post-bombardment reconstruction can create structures absent from the imagery underlying ML frames. ML-only frames produce systematic coverage error, and targeted satellite validation can reduce it.

title: Workplace Mental Health and Psychological Safety: A Systematic Review of Interventions and Outcomes
abstract: Background. Workplace mental health and psychological safety are critical determinants of employee wellbeing, organizational performance, and public health. Despite growing recognition of their importance, evidence on effective interventions across occupational sectors remains fragmented, and the moderating role of psychosocial safety climate (PSC) is underexplored in existing syntheses. Objective. This systematic review synthesizes global evidence on individual- and organizational-level workplace mental health interventions, with particular attention to psychological safety climate as a moderating construct and the differential effectiveness of universal versus targeted delivery models. Methods. A comprehensive, PRISMA 2020-compliant search was conducted across PubMed and Google Scholar databases, covering publications from 2011 to 2026. Ninety-seven records were identified; following removal of four duplicates, 93 deduplicated records were retained, encompassing systematic reviews, meta-analyses, umbrella reviews, and qualitative syntheses. Quality appraisal employed ROBINS-I, QATQS, AXIS, Downs and Black, GRADE, and EPHPP tools. Results. Individual-level digital interventions demonstrated the strongest measurable short-term effects: mindfulness-based eHealth programs (Hedge’s g = 0.60) outperformed cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT; g = 0.15) and stress management programs (g = 0.17). Web-based interventions improved psychological wellbeing (g = 0.37) and work effectiveness (g = 0.25), with effects sustained at follow-up (g = 0.23). Targeted delivery yielded markedly larger effects for stress management (g = 0.64–0.69) compared to universal delivery (g = 0.00). Universal CBT reduced depression across the general workforce (SMD = 0.16). Manager training significantly increased mental health knowledge (SMD = 0.73). Among healthcare workers during the COVID-19 pandemic, pooled disorder prevalence reached 36% for depression, 37% for PTSD, 27% for stress, 47% for anxiety, and 49% for insomnia. Organizational-level interventions showed mixed results with high heterogeneity. Conclusions. Effective workplace mental health promotion requires multi-layered strategies that combine scalable digital tools with organizational structural changes and manager capability building. Future research should prioritize longitudinal designs, under-represented worker populations, cost-effectiveness analyses, and the integration of PSC measurement into intervention frameworks.

title: Resilient Citizens in Resilient Societies: The Determinants of Individuals’ Resilience
abstract: Structural change and recurrent crises are causing major disruptions to societies and citizens. There- fore, both policy-makers and scientists widely encourage strengthening individuals’ resilience. But social science resilience-literature is often criticized for ambivalent conceptualization and limited policy-applicability. We therefore aim at identifying the determinants of individuals’ resilience while addressing these shortcomings. Our theoretical framework conceptualizes resilience in terms of empirically testable life-course capitals that help individuals maintain desired outcomes by meeting changed resource-needs and reduced resource-access during disturbances. These life-course capitals include not only an individual’s economic and human capital, but also their social capital (from meso-level social networks) and “institutional capital” (support from macro-level public institutions). As such these capitals are multi-dimensional, multi-level, and interacting. Our empirical analysis employs multi-level regression models using longitudinal individual-level (n=16,071) and country-level data across 23 European countries during the COVID-19 pandemic. We find all life-course capital variables – lower economic arrears, savings, housing insecurity, education, health, social inclusion, public social expenditure, and government effectiveness – are positively associated with individual resilience. Social inclusion matters most, followed by health. We also find substitution-effects between life-course capitals. Life-course capitals explain a total of 22% of the resilience-variance – explain- ing around 45% of the between-country(-group) variance (1-2% of the total variance), 36% of the between-individual variance (62%), and practically no within-individual resilience-variance (37%). Associations are rather stable across country-groups, but in Southern Europe social inclusion, education, and institutional capital matter slightly more. These findings suggest that a multi-dimensional policy approach – prioritizing social inclusion and public health while considering country-specific conditions – can be promising.

title: Fertility, Affiliation Transmission, and Religious Reproduction in Germany
abstract: Religious groups reproduce across generations through childbearing and the transmission of affiliation. I examine how these processes jointly shape religious composition in Germany. A pseudo-prospective design combines repeated cross-sectional surveys of women’s affiliation and fertility with retrospective information on maternal affiliation and adult offspring affiliations from the German Socio-Economic Panel. I reconstruct five-group distributions for women born in 1931-1950 and their offspring, including childless women in the starting population. Under the assumptions linking these sources, fertility differences modify but do not reverse the generational redistribution associated with affiliation transmission. Catholic point estimates indicate partial fertility compensation for transmission losses, whereas Protestant fertility provides little compensation. Lower fertility moderates but does not eliminate unaffiliated gains. Across maternal cohorts, the unaffiliated generational gap narrows as the maternal share rises toward a comparatively stable reconstructed offspring share. Unaffiliated mothers also account for a growing share of unaffiliated offspring. A conditional reconstruction for women born in 1951-1970 yields the same directions in the point estimates under fixed transmission probabilities. The findings quantify the limited extent of fertility compensation in the reconstructed religious reproduction of these cohorts.

title: Immigrant wages are lower in immigrant-dense areas, and the limited-English differential is mostly occupational: metropolitan Philadelphia, 2012–2024
abstract: Immigrants who speak limited English earn less than those who speak it well. On the protective view of residential concentration, that differential should be smaller where immigrants are concentrated, because concentration supplies employers and customers who do not require English. On the isolation view it should be larger. This study tests both views in metropolitan Philadelphia, a former gateway whose immigrant population has grown again, with American Community Survey microdata for 2012 to 2024 and a two-level model of 7,355 foreign-born workers in 48 Public Use Microdata Areas. Hourly wages are about 8 percent lower per standard deviation of area immigrant density for foreign-born workers who speak English well and about 3 percent lower, an estimate not distinguishable from zero, for those who speak it poorly. Native-born workers in the same areas show a gradient of 2 percent, so most of the difference is specific to immigrants. The interaction between density and limited English is 0.049 (standard error 0.029) and disappears once occupation is held constant. The limited-English differential is 21 percent overall and 9 percent within an occupation, so most of it is associated with the occupations limited-English workers hold. An exploratory measure of the density of the worker’s own home language gives a positive interaction of 0.046 (0.022), driven by lower wages for proficient workers rather than higher wages for limited-English workers, and the same specification in the New York metropolitan area gives 0.045 (0.009). Higher earners move from the city to the suburbs.

title: List and Sequential Attention
abstract: This paper studies stochastic choice when both availability and presentation order may vary across choice problems. We characterize a fixed-list sequential attention model for menu choice and a sequential attention model with a common continuation profile for list choice. In the list domain, we further show that, holding preferences fixed, more persistent attention shifts choice probability toward more preferred alternatives.

title: AI Systems for Filmmaking: A Survey of HCI Research from a Labor-Centered Perspective
authors: YUYING TANG, Lin Gao, Haotian Li, Baiqiao Zhang, Rebecca Fiebrink, Sebastian Deterding, Xiaojuan Ma, Huamin Qu
abstract: Artificial intelligence is integrated into filmmaking and has attracted attention in human-computer interaction (HCI). Existing studies have primarily characterized AI systems for filmmaking by their capabilities and supported tasks, with limited attention to the organisation of filmmaking labor during system use. We review 31 HCI system papers and develop a three-layer taxonomy of labor sites, labor types, and human-AI allocation, examining where AI systems are positioned, what types of labor are involved during system use, and how those labor types are allocated between humans and AI. Our analysis reveals a concentration on individual below-the-line contexts, increasing attention to structural and meaning-making labor beyond execution, comparatively limited relational labor, and substantial variation in human-AI allocation across labor types. We further identify opportunities for the design and evaluation of AI systems that account for the broader organization of filmmaking labor. This review provides a labor-centered taxonomy for synthesizing AI systems for filmmaking and a basis for examining how AI may become involved in broader organizations of creative labor.

title: Who Speaks When the Chatbot Answers? Generative AI as Institutional Speech
authors: Bibhor Acharya, Sandesh Gupta, Himani Moktan
abstract: When a branded chatbot answers a customer, the reply is often taken as the institution speaking. This paper treats that uptake as a media and communication problem rather than as a model-accuracy problem alone. Using Erving Goffman’s account of footing—the gap between who animates an utterance and who stands as its principal—and Austin and Searle’s account of commitments as speech acts, we read the British Columbia Civil Resolution Tribunal decision in Moffatt v. Air Canada (2024 BCCRT 149) as a public episode of institutional speech gone wrong. A website chatbot told Jake Moffatt that a bereavement fare could be claimed retroactively within ninety days; a different page on the same site, and later human staff, denied that path. Air Canada argued it should not be held liable for the chatbot; the tribunal disagreed and ordered damages. The case lets us follow authorization, utterance, uptake, contested repair, and the failed attempt to split the animator from the principal. While systematic reviews of AI disadvantages map privacy, displacement, and bias at a macroeconomic scale, they leave open this micro-communicative surface where an institution’s name is attached to a fluent reply. We argue that handoff to a named human is part of the speech act when commitment is at stake, not an optional engineering fallback.

title: Consumer-level Virtual Reality Applications and Users' Wellbeing: The Role of Problematic Use, Social Support, Harassment, and the Medium's Affordances
abstract: Virtual Reality (VR) applications are increasingly adopted by consumers for gaming, social interaction, and other purposes, raising questions about their impact on users' wellbeing. Against this backdrop, this study explores the associations between experiences of problematic use, social support, and harassment during the use of consumer-level VR applications and users' wellbeing-related variables, as well as how the affordances of these applications may facilitate each of these mechanisms. We conducted a pre-registered online survey (N = 717) with VR users of a diverse range of applications. Results showed that perceived social support obtained in VR environments was a positive predictor of both wellbeing and life satisfaction, while harassment was a negative predictor of life satisfaction. While a bivariate correlation existed between screen time and users' wellbeing, it disappeared once these experiential variables were accounted for, suggesting that what happens during VR use matters more than how long it lasts. Social presence and embodiment while using VR were positively associated with problematic use, social support, and (social presence only) harassment, while moderation affordances were positively associated with social support. Loot boxes emerged as a robust predictor of problematic use, extending gambling-adjacent reward mechanics documented in conventional gaming to VR specifically. These findings provide a first quantitative, integrated approach to factors that have so far been studied mainly from a qualitative standpoint or in isolation, supporting a shift away from dose-response models of VR's effects toward affordance- and mechanism-based frameworks.

title: The Ranma ½ Effect: Why the Same Aggression Does Not Look Equally Dangerous
abstract: This paper develops the ‘Ranma ½ Effect,’ a testable theoretical account of why identical or substantively similar aggressive behavior may be perceived as more or less dangerous depending on the social configuration in which it occurs. The discussion begins with recurring forms of comic punishment in Japanese popular culture, including Ranma 1/2, and connects them to existing research on humor, gender, intimate partner violence, anger expression, leadership, organizational silence, and employee voice.
