Prior findings are mixed: aggression toward male targets is sometimes judged as less serious, whereas women who express anger in professional settings can be evaluated more negatively than men. Rather than treating these findings as contradictory, this paper argues that perceived dangerousness is configuration-dependent. Gender, age, status, experience, physical formidability, prior reputation, relational context, cultural framing, and observer norms jointly shape whether an act is interpreted as aggression, strictness, guidance, punishment, or simply “the way that person is.” Two workplace observations are used as theory-generating illustrations. In one setting, strong public corrective behavior by a highly competent and positively regarded manager coexisted with favorable evaluations of competence and leadership. In another, a comparatively young manager coordinated older, experienced workers without relying on anger as a primary control resource. These observations are used to construct a counterfactual comparison in which the conduct is held constant while the actor-target configuration is altered, providing a basis for future vignette experiments. The central argument is that social judgments of aggression are shaped not only by what is done, but also by who does it to whom and under what relational and cultural conditions. Such perceptual differences may affect third-party intervention, corrective feedback, and the continued use or normalization of aggressive managerial behavior. The danger of the Ranma ½ Effect lies not only in making aggression acceptable, but in making aggression less recognizable as aggression.

title: Algorithmic Serendipity, Excessive Scrolling, and Creative Thinking in Short-Form Video Consumption: A Theoretical Review.
abstract: Short form videos from different apps have become popular ways for entertainment and relaxation. It has transformed digital media consumption through personalized recommendations and rapid content delivery. This theoretical review examines the relationship between algorithmic serendipity, excessive scrolling and creativity in short-form video consumption. This review proposes two interconnected pathways. One suggests that unexpected and relevant algorithmic recommendation may generate curiosity and anticipation of future discoveries encouraging continuous scrolling. Second path suggests that exposure to diverse information, ideas and perspectives may support creative thinking, at the same time, prolonged exposure and continuous scrolling reduces sustained attention and deeper cognitive processing required for creativity. Thus, algorithmic serendipity may represent double edge process. The review provides a theoretical basis for future empirical research examining the conditions under which algorithmic created video consumption may support or hinder creative thinking.

title: The Counter Monster: How Organizational Pressure Is Eaten and Converted into Knowledge, External Value, and Persistence
abstract: This paper develops a theoretical model explaining why organizational pressure does not always produce silence, compliance, or exit. Existing research on employee voice, organizational silence, whistleblowing, abusive supervision, job embeddedness, and resilience has extensively examined how employees respond to unfavorable organizational conditions. Less attention, however, has been paid to situations in which pressure itself becomes material for observation, documentation, comparison, theorization, and external value creation, and in which that value subsequently feeds back into the actor’s capacity to remain autonomous from internal organizational evaluation. The paper introduces the concept of the Counter Monster and identifies Pressure-Eating as its core mechanism. Pressure-Eating refers to the process through which organizational pressure is experienced not only as psychological or occupational loss but also as information containing contradictions, repetitions, institutional responses, and changes in organizational explanations that can later be analyzed. The concept does not imply that pressure becomes harmless. Rather, damage and information may coexist. The paper further develops Cross-Domain Incentive Inversion to describe situations in which an event carrying negative value within the organization acquires different value in external domains such as research, professional practice, legal processes, or external networks. When this conversion occurs, pressure intended or experienced as increasing the cost of staying may simultaneously generate new observational or knowledge value. This possibility is conceptualized as the Exit Pressure Paradox. The recursive connection among organizational pressure, Pressure-Eating, knowledge production, external value, reduced dependence on internal evaluation, persistence, and further organizational responses is theorized as the Counter Loop. The Counter Monster is treated not as a stable personality type but as an actor-state emerging from the interaction of resilience, autonomy, analytical capacity, externalization capacity, and the availability of external value arenas. Generative AI is positioned not as the cause of the Counter Monster but as an external cognitive medium that can reduce the costs of documentation, comparison, literature connection, drafting, translation, and externalization. Finally, the paper proposes the Boring Organization Principle: organizations are more likely to weaken the Counter Loop by maintaining fair procedures, explainable decisions, revisability, and ordinary treatment than by escalating exceptional control. The theory does not celebrate adversity or harassment; it argues instead that organizations cannot fully control the meaning and downstream value of the pressure they impose.

title: An Exploratory Study On The Presentation Of News On Select Print Media Using Framing Analysis
abstract: This study explores the presentation and framing of the Koodankulam Nuclear Power Plant (KKNPP) protest in two leading English-language newspapers in Tamil Nadu, The Hindu and The New Indian Express. The study examines how mainstream print media selected, emphasized, and presented different dimensions of the protest and how these framing patterns contributed to the construction of public discourse. A comparative content analysis was conducted on news reports published during September 2012, focusing on coverage of the KKNPP protest in the Tirunelveli and Chennai editions of the selected newspapers. Framing theory, particularly the conceptual framework associated with Erving Goffman and Robert Entman, was employed to identify and analyze dominant, causes, and definitions frames. The study examined frames including de-legitimizing, legitimizing, injustice, sympathy, contextual, state/court reinforcement, human rights violations, freedom of expression, targeting marginalized groups, external influence, environmental considerations, unrest, uprising, protest, conspiracy, and chaos. The findings indicate differences between the two newspapers in several framing categories. Significant differences were observed in selected frames, including de-legitimizing, sympathy, contextual, protest, conspiracy, and chaos, while other frames showed comparatively limited differences. The study concludes that mainstream print media coverage of the KKNPP protest was not uniform and that the framing of the issue shifted across different stages of the protest, particularly from state/court reinforcement towards human rights and freedom-of-expression perspectives. The findings highlight the importance of examining news selection, emphasis, and framing in understanding the construction of media narratives surrounding social movements and public controversies.

title: Cricket as Entertainment and Politics in India
authors: Ramprasath P S, Dr. Manikkam K
abstract: Cricket in India is not a sport; it is part of entertainment and politics. This study considers the working of cricket both as enjoyment and as a political tool. It shows how cricket has moved from a colonial sport to a powerful platform for image-making, branding, and international relations with the help of media and prominent people. The following study adopts a qualitative approach by analysing books, interviews, and content on three broad issues: the use of cricket as a prop by politicians, especially through the IPL, for image building; increased participation through fantasy leagues and digital platforms; and cricket as something more than just a game. Strong institutions, like the BCCI, are found instrumental in connecting cricket to politics. Media frames people's interpretation of cricket and often presents it as an icon of wealth, youth, and development while masking several aspects of political and commercial influence over cricket. The study further reveals that caste, nepotism, and family relationships are also linked with the interpretation of cricket as entertainment. The present research argues that cricket is not merely a source of entertainment but also a political gadget. It is a site where debates and contests over national identity, social cohesion, and political authority are being conducted. The implications of the study are immense on media, culture, and sports management.

title: From Public Objection to Standing and Back: Mediated Public Authorization
abstract: How can practices that sustain a public concern change who is entitled to pursue it? This article develops Mediated Public Authorization, a framework connecting public persistence with practical standing. It specifies two contingent mechanisms: mediated objections become usable grounds for allocating standing, and implemented allocations enter production practices that reorganise subsequent questioning. Public renewal depends on participants using those arrangements. A hypothetical service controversy shows how these connections differ from exposure, source visibility, favourable reception and administrative change alone. Drawing on research on media standing, mediated political interaction, representation and publicness, the framework traces participant-linked claim passages and distinguishes entitlements from obligations to answer. It proposes conditional expectations about contextual retrieval, evidentiary transmission, entitlement reproduction and renewed questioning. It also specifies a pathway to institutional adaptation and a benchmark for inequality in new entitlement grants. MPA examines how a concern can remain publicly contestable as its speakers, constituencies and routes of pursuit change.

title: The Quiet Male: Exploring Silence and Masculinity in Jaggi (2022)
abstract: This investigation concerns that the story of the film revolves around the inferiority and marginalization of the protagonist, Jaggi (2022), whose failure to execute heterosexual virility is a direct opposition to the local organization of hegemonic masculinity of physical toughness, aggressiveness, and unchallenged sexual potency (Naahar, 2024). The consequent silence of Jaggi (2022) (his inability to express his trauma, protect on behalf of those that fail to meet the hegemonic concept) individual people that do not match the hegemonic standard. This discussion puts R.W.CONNELL to himself, or challenge the rumours is hypothesized as a symptom of his subordinated masculine status. It is not an individual trait but a structural impairment, and reveals the emotional price of masculinity (Connell and Messerschmidt, 200 Connell theory of Hegemonic Masculinity (Connell, 1995) to explore how the theme of silence is unified in the Punjabi film Jaggi (2022) (2022). The movie, which unfolds the story of a rural schoolboy that is victimized by the harassment of unstoppable bullies and was labeled a homosexual due to his inability to procreate, is interpreted as the vivid depiction of violence required to realize an idealized masculinity. The paper focuses on the patriarchal enforcing of the gender order by the hegemonic men characters of the movie the bullies and the patriarch family of Jaggi (2022) through the use of violence and cultural exclusion. Their violent and noisy shows are contrasted with the silent suffering of Jaggi (2022) to remind us of the disciplining nature of hegemonic masculinity in imposing gender obedience on men. This deadly aspect of this repressive gender regime is demonstrated by the fateful choice that Jaggi (2022) made in the end. Jaggi (2022) is therefore an interesting case study of the way that hegemonic masculinity is perpetuated via the discursive and affective act of erasing other forms of masculinity and in this regard, silence becomes a loquid signifier of systemic violence.

title: Femme Fatale in Tamil Cinema: An Analysis of Varalaxmi Sarathkumar’s Antagonistic Characterization in Sarkar (2018) and Sandakozhi 2 (2018)
abstract: Feminist film theory and the concept of femme fatale have been adopted as the theoretical underpinning of this study. The present study aims to understand and explore the concept of femme fatale and its manifestation through the female antagonists in the movies Sarkar and Sandakozhi 2. Generally, women in Tamil cinema have had little scope as antagonists, being relegated to supporting and romantic interests within patriarchal narratives. Recent Tamil cinema has, however, started to offer more nuanced and complex female antagonists who break away from traditional gender constructs. The present study aims to explore and understand the concept of femme fatale and its manifestation through the female antagonists in the movies Sarkar (2018) and Sandakozhi 2 (2018) portrayed by Varalaxmi Sarathkumar. The present study aims to understand and explore how the concept of femme fatale is represented in the movies Sarkar and Sandakozhi 2.

title: The 128 Paths to Victory - Swing State Math in the U.S. Presidential Elections
authors: N. Asger Mortensen, Joel D. Cox
abstract: In U.S. presidential elections, outcomes are often predictable in most states, with variability primarily introduced by a small number of "swing states". While the specific swing states can fluctuate from one election cycle to the next, they collectively play a critical role in determining the overall result. In the 2024 election, seven key swing states contribute a total of 93 delegates to the electoral college. Without considering mutual correlations, each of the 128 potential electoral outcomes has an equal probability of approximately 0.8%. Due to an uneven distribution of "safe" delegates (219 Republican and 226 Democrat), the Democratic candidate holds a slight statistical advantage. Analysing all possible outcomes for the 2024 election suggests an estimated 55% probability for a Democratic win, compared to 42% for a Republican victory. The odds of a tie are approximately 2.3%, while the likelihood of either party achieving a clean sweep of all swing states is 0.8%. A detailed analysis of the 128 possible election outcomes reinforces the widely held view that securing Pennsylvania is crucial to electoral success. Notably, in 4\% of all possible scenarios, victory is achieved by the narrowest possible margin, and in every such case, it hinges on winning Pennsylvania.

title: "I don't give a shit anymore" – Future-Oriented Career Agency and Precarity at the Postdoc Stage
authors: Julian Hamann, Kathia Serrano Velarde, Tim Fenkner, Jonas Gottschalk-Rayling, Sven Boniger, Michi Hügel
abstract: This paper examines how postdoctoral researchers navigate precarious employment conditions and claim career agency during an uncertain career stage. Drawing on a longitudinal qualitative interview panel of 35 postdocs from particle physics and modern history, the study distinguishes between two forms of agency: empowered strategizing and restricted drifting. Strategizing postdocs actively align short- to mid-term career goals with opportunities arising from fixed-term contracts and grant funding cycles, while drifting postdocs prioritize present research activities over long-term planning. Through in-depth interviews conducted in three waves, the analysis reveals how temporal horizons are compressed by the cyclical nature of academic recruitment and funding. The findings highlight the dynamic interplay between structural constraints and different forms of individual agency. This work contributes a processual perspective on career agency and precarity and adds to career research and studies of precarious working conditions.

title: Measuring the impact of area-based early years support in Wales on children’s social care: Preliminary findings
authors: Meng Le Zhang, Martin Elliott, Gareth Griffith, Sally Holland
abstract: Flying Start is an area-based intervention which offers support for families with children under four living in disadvantaged areas in Wales. This study uses a quasi-experiment (Regression Discontinuity Design) and administrative data on children born in Wales between 2012 and 2017 (n = 126,705) to measure the impact of Flying Start eligibility on children’s social care at age 4/5. We find that Flying Start reduces rates of children with care and support plans and children looked after. These effects are stronger for male infants and mothers who were 21 or younger at childbirth. However, we find no effects on child protection.

title: Answering without disclosing: How officials under scrutiny compress what they say
abstract: How do organisational actors withhold information while continuing to answer under scrutiny? Research on organisational silence has largely treated withholding as a question of whether actors speak. This article examines variation within speech through 1 781 question-and-answer exchanges from 102 recorded interview encounters with senior officials in prison health governance across three studies conducted between 2016 and 2023. Narrative absence was coded across six features and response timing was derived from audio and validated against blinded listener judgements. Higher narrative absence was associated with substantially shorter answers within encounters, and this association held across all robustness checks. Changes in response onset were much smaller, while pausing supported no independent association, and the automated measure of fillers and repairs failed validation. The findings identify controlled compression as a response form through which disclosure contracts while interactional responsiveness continues. Separating responsiveness from disclosure matters because organisational accountability is routinely assessed through visible responsiveness even though meaningful accountability depends on disclosure. An actor may therefore satisfy every observable requirement of cooperation while narrowing what is made available. The article shows that where speaking is expected, withholding does not cease but relocates into the answers themselves.

title: Doubly Preferential: The Treatment of Contested Experts in News Media
authors: François Claveau, Jacob Hamel-Mottiez, Léon Gatien, Olivier Santerre
abstract: This article contributes to the characterization of media bias by analyzing how Canadian news media select and contextualize messages originating from think tanks, an influential yet ideologically marked form of expertise. Drawing on a large media corpus (2017–2021), this article shows that Canadian journalists make relatively limited use of textual indicators of credibility, but that these indicators systematically reflect the ideological preferences already evident in their source selection. Think tanks that are more frequently solicited thus benefit from more favorable contextualization, corroborating the hypothesis of a doubly preferential treatment. The study concludes by discussing the normative implications of these practices for journalistic standards, such as impartiality, in the face of contested expertise.

title: Hate speech against scientists can backfire – but so can counterspeech: Evidence from a four-country experiment
abstract: Hate speech against scientists can harm their well-being and undermine knowledge-based societies, and counterspeech by bystanders is often proposed as a remedy. But comparative evidence on how bystanders perceive hate speech targeting scientists and on whether counterspeech helps is lacking. In a preregistered experiment with quota samples weighted to national population margins from Denmark, Germany, the United Kingdom, and the United States (N = 2,769), participants saw a fictitious social media post by a scientist either alone, with a hateful comment, or with a hateful comment plus a counterspeech reply. Hate speech backfired: Participants rated the scientist’s post more positively in both comment conditions. Counterspeech had mixed effects: It increased participants’ intentions to speak up themselves, but in Germany and the United Kingdom it made the hateful comment appear more acceptable. Our findings advance research on attacks against epistemic authorities and demonstrate the value of comparative, multi-outcome designs.

title: Empathy-Related Traits and Domain-Specific Self-Rated Creativity: Indirect Associations Through Five C-PETS Dimensions
abstract: This study examined statistical indirect associations between empathy-related traits and domain-specific self-rated creativity through five dimensions of the Creative Personality and Thinking Styles Scale (C-PETS). An online survey of 359 North American adults assessed Perspective Taking (PT), Fantasy (FS), and Empathic Concern (EC), the five C-PETS dimensions, and five domains of the Kaufman Domains of Creativity Scale (K-DOCS). Parallel multiple mediation models were estimated using 10,000 bootstrap samples and Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery-rate correction. Significant total indirect effects were found for PT across all five K-DOCS domains, for FS across four domains, and for EC only for Self/Everyday creativity. After correction, significant specific indirect effects were limited to Challenge-Seeking (CS) pathways from PT and FS to all five K-DOCS domains. Because the data were cross-sectional and based on self-report, these results do not establish causal mediation. Instead, they indicate that challenge-seeking is a robust conditional statistical link between perspective-related empathy traits and domain-specific self-rated creativity.

title: From Public Dominance to Private Expansion: Changes in Hospital Infrastructure in Spain (1986–2018)
abstract: In many countries, the growth of the private hospital sector coincides with a decline in beds per inhabitant. Spain is no exception, showing one of the lowest relative bed provisions in the EU. This study offers an exploratory analysis of the evolution of private hospital bed provision in Spain and its Autonomous Communities between 1986 and 2018. Using historical hospital catalogs from the Ministry of Health, we conducted graphical and cluster analyses to examine trends and classify regions by the share of private hospital beds. Results indicate a national trend toward fewer beds and a growing presence of the private, mainly for-profit, sector, with notable regional differences such as the Catalan model. This research provides comparative and long-term evidence on structural changes in Spain’s hospital system.

title: “AI” as gaslighting – Considering the affordances of stochastic generative systems in relation to anthropo-centered epistemic operations
abstract: This paper mobilizes the notion of ‘AI’ as a carcinogen, as developed by Berman, to then inquire and analyze what is the possible human impact that results from the democratization of the use of Large Language Models and Generative Pretrained Transformers, from the perspective of how epistemic frameworks are mobilized as a core component of sociability. It then advances the proposal that we understand ‘AI’ as a case of the ‘Thomas Theorem’, and that, as such, LLMs and GPTs can effectively operate as systems of non-targeted, non-intentional, gaslighting. From that approach, the paper follows up with a materially-grounded analysis of how the operations performed on data for the creation and usage of LLMs and GPTs mean that these technologies have the affordance of being episteme-fixative, and that such an affordance (as defined here) is specific to these technologies, in a way that allows for non-essentialist and non-deterministic analysis that considers both changes and continuities in both media systems and our everyday engagement with them. It concludes by suggesting venues of inquiry that are made easier by the previous conclusions, and returns to capitalism’s uptake of technology, rather than to any immanent aspect of technology, as a central aspect to consider in evaluating the epistemic harms that might come out of these affordances.

title: Using large-scale supermarket transaction data to understand the environmental sustainability and healthiness of food and drink purchases. Policy Insights from the FIO Food Project.
authors: Emma Wilkins, Mark Alan Green, Mark Gilthorpe, Alice Kininmonth, Alexandra Johnstone, Michelle Morris
abstract: A policy brief summarising recommendations for policy from FIO Food work package 2, which uses large-scale retail transaction data to understand the environmental sustainability and healthiness of food and drink purchases.

title: Occupational class inequality in non-monetary job quality in Europe, 1995-2024
abstract: Occupational class is central to research on inequality, but we have limited knowledge about how it structures non-monetary job quality across countries and over time. We examine four dimensions of job quality—autonomy, physical working conditions, work intensity, and work time quality—across eight occupational classes in 14 European countries from 1995 to 2024, using the European Working Conditions Survey. We compare class profiles over time, decompose variation into within- and between-class components, and benchmark occupational class against country, country-year, and income. Most variation in job quality is within occupational classes, but gradients remain pronounced for physical working conditions and autonomy, while work intensity is only weakly structured by class. Cross-national differences are modest on average but substantially larger among lower-skill than higher-skill classes. Occupational class thus remains an important source of inequality in some dimensions of job quality, but captures only part of the broader variation in working conditions.

title: Associations between content and engagement vary across social media communities
abstract: Research on social media engagement often seeks general content features that are associated with online success. However, social media platforms contain communities with different audiences, topics, and norms, and the same features may have different associations with engagement within different communities. This research considers 1,078,044 items from 587 communities in five corpora spanning Reddit, Stack Exchange, X, and YouTube. For each corpus, negativity, moralization, arousal, and in-group versus out-group language were measured. Their relationships with engagement were compared using multilevel models imposing one within-community slope per feature with models allowing slopes to vary across communities. Varying-slope models fit the data better in all five corpora. The estimated community slopes varied substantially in magnitude and, frequently, direction. Nevertheless, the average slopes from the varying-slope models remained small. The improved fit therefore reflects heterogeneity across communities rather than stronger average associations. These findings show that a weak average association can conceal stronger but opposing associations across communities. General claims about the content associated with social media engagement need to account for the specific communities in which that content appears.

title: Attribute Relevance in Conjoint Analysis
abstract: Researchers often rely on conjoint analysis to understand which attributes drive respondents' decisionmaking, yet standard estimands are not designed to measure attribute relevance. We introduce a novel approach to measuring attribute relevance in conjoint analysis by drawing on causal attribution methods. Our proposed estimand, the average probability of necessary and sufficient causation (APNS), captures the probability that swapping two profiles' levels on an attribute would change a respondent's choice. We establish nonparametric identification under assumptions related to preference heterogeneity, and provide simple difference-in-means estimators that can be applied to existing conjoint data structures. Two empirical applications illustrate the method. A candidate choice experiment in Germany reveals significant preference heterogeneity that leads standard estimands to mask relevance, while under the right assumptions the APNS recovers it. By contrast, in a replication of a prominent refugee experiment, we find that assuming preference homogeneity is unproblematic for many attributes of asylum-seekers.

title: BirthClim_IT: A Harmonized Municipality-Level Dataset on Fertility, Environment, and Territorial Contexts in Italy, 2003–2022
abstract: BACKGROUND Environmental conditions and climate change, alongside spatial heterogeneity in fertility, have received increasing attention in fertility research. However, research combining these perspectives remains limited, partly due to the lack of data linking fine spatial resolution with detailed demographic, environmental, and socioeconomic information. This is particularly relevant in Italy, where substantial spatial variation in fertility coexists with heterogeneous environmental conditions. OBJECTIVE This paper introduces BirthClim_IT, a harmonized longitudinal dataset designed to support research on fertility and its environmental and territorial contexts across Italian municipalities. The dataset description is accompanied by two empirical applications illustrating its use. METHODS The BirthClim_IT dataset combines monthly demographic information with environmental, climatic, geographic, and socioeconomic indicators for 7,896 Italian municipalities from January 2003 to December 2022. The dataset contains 126 variables, harmonized to the administrative boundaries in force on January 1, 2024. To address sparsity in monthly birth counts, we also provide a spatially aggregated version comprising 4,936 spatial units and a customizable aggregation procedure. RESULTS The dataset provides both municipality-level and aggregated data, allowing fertility patterns to be examined jointly across space and time. The two descriptive applications illustrate its use in identifying distinct environmental profiles across Italian municipalities and in examining seasonal variation in fertility and environmental conditions. CONTRIBUTION Given the growing interest in environmental dimensions of fertility and increasing attention to the spatial dimension of demographic processes, BirthClim_IT provides a new and flexible resource combining fine spatial and temporal resolution with information spanning multiple dimensions of the demographic, environmental, and socioeconomic context.

title: Scrutiny, sanctions, and attacks on scholars: Public acceptance and perceived deservingness in Switzerland
authors: Niels G. Mede, Julia Metag, Mike S. Schäfer
abstract: Different forms of critical and hostile public engagement with science have been documented worldwide. They range from valuable scrutiny to public protests, support for funding cuts, and attacks. Whether people accept such engagement, and whether they consider it deserved, has rarely been studied with representative data. Using a preregistered, nationally representative survey from Switzerland (n = 698), we examine acceptance of public scrutiny, support for sanctions, and attacks on scholars and their perceived deservingness when scholars speak out politically. We find that acceptance follows a graded hierarchy: Most respondents accept scrutiny, fewer accept sanctions, and hardly anyone accepts attacks. Two thirds consider criticism of politically outspoken scholars deserved, whereas attacks are largely rejected, although noteworthy minorities consider them deserved. Acceptance of attacks is associated with science-related populist attitudes, right-leaning views, younger age, lower income, and active online engagement. Moreover, perceived political distance from scholars is associated with acceptance of scrutiny.

title: Survivors' Perspectives and Experiences of Intimate Partner Violence Perpetrator Intervention Programs and Associated Services: A Qualitative Systematic Review
abstract: This qualitative systematic review synthesises survivors’ perspectives of intimate partner violence perpetrator interventions and associated support services. Specifically, it examines how different relationship structures, such as intact, co-parenting, or separated arrangements, shape these experiences and determines which program features are perceived as supporting or compromising safety. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, electronic databases were searched for peer-reviewed literature published after 1 July 2016. Although 13 studies met the initial inclusion criteria for descriptive mapping, the final thematic synthesis integrated 11 primary sources containing the specific contextual data required for qualitative analysis. The analysis generated three main analytical themes: the intervention environment, perpetrator behaviour patterns, and the survivors’ processing journey. Findings indicate that relationship structures influence how survivors experience these interventions. While individuals navigating ongoing contact or reconciliation attempts often report transactional partner compliance driven by child-access pressures or relationship motivations, those seeking complete separation report an environment of persistent hypervigilance. Survivors report that specialised advocacy and literacy provided by partner contact services support safety by deconstructing mutual-blame frameworks and shifting self blame. Conversely, interventions are perceived as compromising safety when they rely on isolated compliance checks and operate separately from substance use and mental health services, creating a false impression of behavioural change. Ultimately, the qualitative evidence indicates that measuring progress through mere attendance alone provides a misleading indicator of risk, suggesting that future policy should prioritise coordinated communication across sectors and elevate survivor-defined safety as the key indicator of program success.

title: Social media and the prevention or reduction of harmful gambling: a rapid evidence review with integrated lived experience
authors: Jenny Sweetman, Liz Littlewood, Patricia Darcy, Greg Forshaw, Amanda Perry, su golder
abstract: Background and aims: Research has established a clear link between social media use and harmful gambling. Existing systematic reviews highlight how social media platforms enable and normalise gambling. This rapid evidence review aimed to identify interventions using social media to prevent or reduce harmful gambling. Methods: Searches were conducted (January 2026) in MEDLINE, Embase and PsycINFO. Searches of grey literature searches, and backward and forward citations from included references, were also completed. Independent screening, data extraction and quality assessment was undertaken by two independent reviewers. Data were analysed using narrative synthesis methods. An expert by experience group directly informed each stage of the review process. Results: From 1138 unique records, 10 studies met our inclusion criteria (2 randomised controlled trials, 2 cohort studies, 2 mixed methods studies and 4 qualitative studies). Included studies focused on brief messages, the impact of a social media platform outage, and the use of gambling support forums. Findings highlighted the benefits and potential risks of implementing gambling harm reduction strategies on social media, the role of interaction with others, and opportunities to use social media to better understand the process of recovery from problem gambling. Discussion and Conclusions: There is some evidence that social media platforms could usefully support the reduction or prevention of harmful gambling. Further research is required, co-designed by those with lived experience to optimise engagement and impact, to better understand how online interventions can support different people and to assess the effectiveness through large high-quality randomised controlled trials.

title: The Dataset of World Refugee and Asylum Policies (DWRAP): de jure asylum policy for 205 countries, 1951-2022
authors: Christopher W. Blair, Guy Grossman, Jeremy Weinstein
abstract: More than two-thirds of the world's refugees and asylum-seekers are hosted in the developing world, yet the national laws governing their reception have never been measured comprehensively across countries or over time. We introduce the Dataset of World Refugee and Asylum Policies (DWRAP), the most expansive coding of de jure asylum and refugee policy assembled to date. DWRAP records every national law pertinent to forcibly displaced populations in 205 countries from 1951 to 2022---951 legal instruments in all. From the text of each law, we hand-code 54 policy provisions, which we aggregate into 14 strands, five fields---access, services, livelihoods, movement, and participation---and a single index of policy liberality, released in three aggregation forms. The result is a country-year panel of 11,484 observations measuring displacement-policy liberality within and across countries over seven decades. Together, these data open the causes and consequences of refugee-policy change to global, historical analysis. They measure law rather than its enforcement---and so make the distance between the two visible and measurable.

title: Resilience through Pathway Specificity for Managing Climate Shocks. A Review of Evidence from East Africa.
abstract: The study systematically reviews and synthesizes 74 empirical studies from East Africa, covering Ethiopia, Kenya, Somalia, and Somaliland. Using study-level, asset-based thresholds and other complementary indicators, the findings identify that household resilience is non-linear and requires targeted, specific programming. The Pathway-Specific Resilience Framework (PSRF), which the paper validates, divides the target populations into two groups: a resource-deficient group that needs asset assistance and external safety nets (socially supported livelihood resilience pathway) and an asset-based cohort that prioritizes asset protection and market-based interventions. The study found that households with constrained resources face limitations in asset accumulation, which leave them more vulnerable to persistent poverty traps. PSRF proposes poverty graduation that balances immediate protection with long-term resilience through a sequence of protocols. The first “Protocol “A” protects resource-poor (Socially supported pathway) households to prioritize consumption, direct transfers (e.g., assets), and human capital. Once households transition to “Protocol B”, the shift is from survival assistance to access to market, finance, and index-based insurance. Additionally, the PSRF integrates other cross-cutting measures to sustain immediate gains from the protocols and prevent relapses brought by climate shocks. These include basic infrastructure like access to water, healthcare, and education; Connectivity and information such as early warning systems, transport, telecommunications, and adaptation measures including climate-smart technologies. Key words: Pathway-Specific Resilience Framework (PSRF), Drought resilience, livelihood pathways, Social protection, East Africa

title: Commercial video games improve species-related knowledge, perceptions, and action
authors: Katie Blake, Paul J Johnson, Diogo Veríssimo
abstract: Digital media often mediates human-wildlife interactions. It is feared that overexposure to virtual animals will distort public awareness and valuation of real-world species. This is alarming given the current rate of extinction. Commercial video games have attracted much attention for their capacity to engage players with biodiversity and conservation. Yet their impact for this is unclear. We use an online experiment to explore whether this medium can improve species-related knowledge, perceptions, and actions, as well as test assumptions that digitised wildlife are favoured by players over real-world counterparts. Our findings are based on a sample of 272 players and 273 non-players of Planet Zoo, using species that feature in this title. We found that both gameplay hours and recency of playing Planet Zoo are positively linked to: more accurately identifying species’ names and conservation status; how much the species are liked; threat appraisals about the likelihood and impact of species loss; and increased donations. Players donated nearly twice as much to species protection as non-players on average (£7.16 versus £4.68), and they allocated the maximum possible donation value of £20 three times as often. Furthermore, we did not observe any detrimental outcomes for digitised wildlife on responses compared to real versions, and we found that any positive effects from experience with Planet Zoo tended to be greater for reptiles than mammals. Our findings do not support concerns that digital media necessarily has harmful implications for public engagement with biodiversity and conservation. Rather, we show that commercial video games might provide an avenue for players to better understand the natural world and take action to protect it, and they might even be particularly beneficial for less desirable taxa. We challenge more game studios to bridge the gap between virtual and real nature where appropriate, joining efforts to ensure that wildlife can also persist beyond digital spaces. We encourage more researchers to pursue this line of inquiry. Given the rapid loss of biodiversity, we cannot continue to overlook how these platforms with global reach might be leveraged to drive conservation action.

title: ‘Building the Internationalist City from Below’: The Role of the Czechoslovak Industrial Cooperative “Interhelpo” in Forging Urbanity in early-Soviet Bishkek
abstract: Abstract The paper explores the historical trajectory of Interhelpo, an industrial cooperative from Czechoslovakia, and its role in forging urbanization “from below” in early-Soviet town of Pishpek (now Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan). In light of scarce literature available on the success and failures of Western internationalist communes in the early Soviet period, this paper draws from intensive field work in Kyrgyzstan and understudied sources in Czech, Kyrgyz, Slovak and Russian to offer a novel, bottom-up narrative on the socialist city in Central Asia. Founded 1924 by Czech, Slovak, Hungarian, German internationalists and Ido-learners around the mountaineer and Bolshevik Rudolf Pavlovič Mareček in the Czechoslovakian town Žilina, the cooperative actively shaped urbanization in what would be become known as the capital of Soviet Kyrgyzstan. From 1925 until its liquidation during WWII, the cooperative built from scratch a whole district including the first electric power station of the city, textile and furniture factories, workshops for tailors, shoemakers and joiners, a school, a kindergarten, a tannery, a brewery as well as unique residential district. In the process, the cooperative forged an organic patchwork language referred to as spontánne esperanto to secure translocal collaboration between internationalists from Central Europe, on the one hand, and a heterogeneous mix of workers including Armenians, Kyrgyz, Dungans, Uygurs, Uzbeks, Russians and Ukrainians, on the other. Transcending a purely historical analysis, the paper ultimately turns to the urban landscape of present-day Bishkek. There it argues that while the district built by Interhelpo corresponds today to an exiled site dislocated by the hegemonic ethno-national memory regime, its materiality harbors relicts of another future capable of mobilizing alternative narratives on the city and her socialist and multi-ethnic past.

title: Research dataset sharing and ethical researcher conduct: A commentary on Ghuge et al. (2026) and Kumar et al. (2026).
authors: Margaret K. Merga, Saiyidi Mat Roni
abstract: This commentary is written for an audience within and beyond academia, as it concerns a dataset from the international community of school library professionals (SLPs). After briefly orienting the reader to commentary and data fabrication, we respond to Ghuge et al. (2026) and Kumar et al. (2026), recent articles with the same corresponding author. Kumar et al. (2026) strongly imply that amongst other researchers, there was a fabrication of data in our 2026 article where some SLP respondents disclosed experiencing significant risk related to their work roles, notably though not exclusively in the US political context. Kumar et al.’s (2026) “reasonable evidence” that we fabricated our data is based on our data availability statement and an opinion poll sent to associates (N=100); this method does not test whether a dataset exists. Ghuge et al. (2026) cites Kumar et al., (2026) to make a similar though far softer claim. We consider Kumar et al. (2026) in relation to ethical conduct in research methods and research respondent risk related to research ecosystem norms. Data sharing cannot be simply conflated with ethical research conduct. If we cannot guarantee anonymity where appropriate, at-risk populations will refuse to participate in social science research.

title: A Productivity Fixated World in the Age of AI: Investigating The Purpose of Human Art
abstract: Modern society increasingly prioritizes final products over the creative process, a trend exacerbated by the rapid adoption of generative AI. This study aims to explore the impact of AI integration into the creative process on subjective well-being and fulfillment, and to determine whether these effects differ between individuals creating for leisure versus those creating for a profession. Within this research, a quantitative-focused survey was conducted with 200 adults, categorized using a 2x2 design: acting as either a hobbyist or a professional illustrator, and either utilizing or not utilizing AI. The data reveals a consistent drop in a person’s well-being across both hobbyist and professional groups when AI is utilized. The differences in fulfillment between hobbyist and professional groups were not statistically significant. While a positive correlation was found between a product-focused mindset and satisfaction among professionals using AI, the overall satisfaction for AI users across the board remained significantly lower than for those who didn’t use AI. These findings suggest that AI integration into creative tasks carries measurable psychological costs by separating the creator from the intrinsically beneficial creative process, along with social costs that taint the creator-audience relationship. These findings underscore the value of human creation, suggesting that the ongoing conversation surrounding AI adoption must extend beyond efficiency to account for value within the human process. An avenue for further research lies within AI use in other fields less traditionally considered a “creative” discipline, such as STEM, which show evidence of having similar psychological benefits arising from the process.

title: Understanding First Nations Disconnection and Reimagining Connection: A yarn between Aboriginal women.
abstract: Connection and belonging are significant processes concerning cultural identity, and for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples in Australia, it has been at the forefront of discussions around the Social and Emotional Wellbeing of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people. One area that needs more investigation is that of those individuals on the margins of society who may find access to communities a complex practice. Furthermore, there has been an emergence of recent practices that move connection and belonging beyond more traditional ways of being towards modernity, which includes inclusiveness, accessibility and flexibility for those involved. Drawing on existing literature, collaborative yarning with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples and reflective commentary, this article explores the many facets of connection and belonging and the ways in which many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples navigate between cultural traditions, socio-historical challenges and contemporary realities. We call for a reimagining of community spaces and practices to ensure they are inclusive and responsive to the diversity of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples’ lived experiences.

title: Do Chatbots Sound Equally Sure in French and in Arabic? A Pilot Audit of Expressed Certainty in ChatGPT and Gemini
abstract: People increasingly ask chatbots about health and public services and pass the answers on to others. Whether they check first may depend on how sure an answer sounds. This pilot audit asks whether the certainty cues that chatbots give change with the language of the question. Ten questions on public health and public services in Morocco were asked once in French and once in Modern Standard Arabic to ChatGPT and Gemini (40 answers). Answers were scored with a bilingual lexicon of hedges and boosters. Both chatbots hedged less in Arabic than in French, and the pattern held under two alternative versions of the lexicon. A model-assisted second coding of 10 answers showed that the lexicon captured boosters well but missed about a third of hedges. With 10 questions and one run each, these results are a first look, not a finding. They motivate a larger audit with repeated runs and human validation.

title: Fairness Perception and Trust Erosion in Competitive Mobile Gaming: A Five-Year Longitudinal Study of a Persian-Language Backgammon Platform
abstract: Fairness perception is a critical yet understudied dimension of player experience in competitive mobile games. This paper presents findings from a five-year longitudinal qualitative study (2022–2026) examining how players construct, reinforce, and communicate beliefs about unfairness in a competitive mobile gaming environment. Using Inductive Thematic Analysis (ITA), we analysed a corpus of more than 52,000 player reviews collected across multiple mobile app marketplaces, supplemented by anonymised customer support interaction transcripts obtained through a research collaboration agreement. Data were collected using a longitudinal sampling design that examined the same calendar month across five consecutive years, enabling the identification of long-term trends while reducing seasonal effects. Analysis identified seven operational themes describing players’ fairness-related beliefs and behaviours, which were subsequently consolidated into three higher-order meta-themes: Perceived Agency (the belief that game systems determine outcomes independently of player skill), Trust Erosion (the progressive reinforcement of manipulation beliefs through negative experiences and platform interactions), and Statistical Misinterpretation (the attribution of probabilistic outcomes to intentional system design). The proportion of 1-star reviews citing fairness-related concerns increased from 3% in 2022 to 18% in 2026, indicating a substantial decline in player trust over the study period. The study further proposes a ten-stage Player Journey of Distrust, mapping the cognitive and emotional progression from initial doubt to entrenched beliefs about manipulation. Findings suggest that fairness complaints are often better understood as expressions of deteriorating trust rather than perceptions of technical malfunction. The paper discusses implications for transparency design, player communication strategies, support systems, and the broader study of trust in digital gaming environments. Keywords: fairness perception; player experience; trust erosion; mobile gaming; thematic analysis; player psychology; app store reviews; cognitive bias; longitudinal qualitative research; trust in digital systems

title: Assaults, Self-Harm, and the Allocation of State Resources in English and Welsh Prisons, 2009-2010 to 2024-2025
abstract: Routine prison allocation in England and Wales is based on staffing, occupancy and regime, but does not incorporate assaults or self-harm. Using 1,727 public-sector establishment-years of Ministry of Justice expenditure and safety data from 2009-2010 to 2024-2025, this article examines whether deteriorating conditions were followed by changes in expenditure. Real expenditure per place fell 28.7 per cent by 2016-2017 before recovering, while prisons retained their relative positions. Higher assault rates were associated with increased expenditure in the following year before 2019-2020, but not thereafter; the interaction test did not establish a change between periods. Self-harm showed no statistically detectable association with subsequent expenditure in either period. Routine allocation continued throughout, but did not consistently respond to deteriorating safety conditions.

title: Reference Observability and Journal Universe Choice in Open Reconstructions of Recursive Journal Metrics
abstract: Open reconstructions of recursive journal indicators can differ from a benchmark along two dimensions: reference observability, which determines which citation records enter the calculation, and the recursive journal universe, over which prestige circulates. We analyze the two dimensions separately in a factorial design. First, we reconstruct Clarivate’s 2024 Article Influence Score (AIS) with OpenAlex data as the Article Network Score (ANS) for a JCR-derived universe (J), the Norwegian Register (N), and the OpenAlex journal universe (A), with ANS defined for 21,706, 22,577, and 107,268 journals, respectively. Then, using a common sample of 15,951 journals, we cross the three universes with two treatments: RAW includes all cited-window articles and reviews, whereas REF retains only those for which OpenAlex records at least one reference. REF improves agreement with AIS in every universe: mean error falls and rank agreement rises. An additional component experiment shows that this improvement does not come from changing the ANS denominator alone, but from its joint change with citation-edge eligibility. Across universes, J and N yield similar results, whereas A has consistently higher errors and lower rank agreement. Robustness checks support the main results on larger journal sets, in the Leiden/CWTS core universe, and in 2023.

title: "They Caught Us Without Any Reason": Waste Pickers' Encounters with Police, Crime and the State in Rawalpindi–Islamabad, Pakistan
abstract: Informal waste pickers (rag-pickers) are routinely portrayed as a source of urban crime, yet little research asks how they themselves experience the police, the state and the illicit economies around them. Drawing on semi-structured interviews in Urdu with 25 waste pickers aged roughly 10 to 50, living in informal settlements (katchi abadis) in Rawalpindi and Islamabad, Pakistan, this article examines their encounters with law-enforcement bodies, their involvement in and victimisation by crime, and their access to government and NGO support. Thematic analysis, informed by street-level bureaucracy and general strain theory, identified four themes: (1) extractive policing, with arbitrary detention, bribes as the price of release, and police ties to employers and dealers; (2) crime as coerced and relational, with drug use and sex work driven by peers, clients, gangs and families; (3) the absent state, with no participant having received government or NGO assistance and BISP applications going unanswered; and (4) constrained pathways into waste picking driven by family need, orphanhood, homelessness and physical incapacity. Most participants said they would leave waste picking if given support. The article calls for protective, non-extractive policing, safeguarding responses to children in sex work and drug use, and outreach that makes social protection reachable. Based on the author's MPhil thesis (National Defence University, Islamabad, 2020). Also archived on Zenodo: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22981971.

title: All-Male Research Samples Discourage Accurate Science Communication
authors: April Bailey, John Dovidio, Jonas R. Kunst, Marilena Juettemeier, Marianne LaFrance, Gulnaz Anjum, Alexander Scott English, Milan Obaidi, David Lackland Sam, Fatma Yaşın Tekizoğlu
abstract: Research samples have historically overrepresented men, resulting in worse outcomes for women. Even when women are represented, inequity might persist due to underlying differences in how people reason about gender. Theories of androcentrism argue that, in general, people emphasize gender more about women than men. Based on this theory and building on prior archival work, we conducted three preregistered experiments (N = 1,315). Participants read scientific findings based either on all-male or all-female samples. For both, the gender homogeneity of the sample is a key limitation that should be noted when describing results. However, participants were more likely to pick women as a keyword to represent findings based on all-female samples (compared to leaving gender unlisted or listing both women and men) than to pick men to describe identical findings based on all-male samples. Grounded in androcentrism theory, this work has practical implications for accurate science communication and gender equity.

title: Research and Impact of Prompt Engineering Nexus on Programming and Routine Tasks: Exploring Future Possible Directions
abstract: Prompt engineering has developed as a transformative subfield in artificial intelligence (AI), enabling humans to enhance AI systems through structured (PROLOG-like) instructions to perform specific tasks. This paper shines a light on its multi-dimensional impact on programming, routine tasks and broader AI applications, drawing on insights from recent studies. By using techniques such as parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT), zero-shot learning, multi-shot learning and linguistic feature analysis, prompt engineering often is used to tackle remaining issues in software engineering (SE), language processing (NLP) and AI safety. The body of literature highlights its role in optimizing AI performance, reducing computational overhead and reducing biases. Additionally, it highlights critical gaps in current methodologies, such as the comparative energy intensity of state-of-art large language models (LLMs) and the requirements for adaptive and scalable prompt crafting strategies. Finally, the paper suggests future directions for research, highlighting the importance of human-centered design and collaboration to advance the field.

title: Unexpected heat suppresses emigration from the world's poorest countries
abstract: Whether climate stress displaces people or traps them in place is unresolved. The common intuition is displacement: crops fail, heat becomes unliveable and people leave. Other work predicts the opposite for poor countries, where migration abroad is expensive and the shock that sharpens the wish to leave can destroy the means to go. Estimates disagree, partly because realized temperature mixes warming that households anticipated with warming they did not. I isolate the unanticipated part with temperature forecast errors, the warmth or cold a forecast missed, and estimate their effect on monthly international migration from countries holding most of the world’s population. Here I show that unexpected warmth does not detectably move migration on average, but that in low-income countries an unexpectedly hot month lowers departures over the following year. No richer income group shows a detectable response. The migration suppression is strongest where incomes depend on agriculture, also appears outside the growing season and leaves in-migration flat, consistent with heat removing the means to move. For the poorest countries, unexpected heat may hold people back rather than push them abroad. Projections and policies built around displacement may overstate departures from these countries and overlook those who cannot afford to leave.

title: Larger, younger, faster, harder: expansion, transformation, and inequality in YouTube’s creator economy (2019–2026)
authors: Bernhard Rieder, Adrian Padilla, Ariadna Matamoros-Fernández, Òscar Coromina
abstract: The growth of YouTube's creator economy raises a question that accounts of individual success and precarity cannot settle: how are the conditions of participation changing across the platform? Comparing two population-scale crawls from 2019 and 2026, we examine expansion, changes in production, and the distribution of attention across millions of channels. The population above the 1,000-subscriber threshold for advertising monetization grew from 4.4 million to 24.5 million, while its video catalogues grew ninefold. Expansion was strongest in South, Southeast, and East Asia, with India's share of channels declaring a country rising from 10 to 27 percent. This growth accompanied substantial turnover: most channels recorded in 2019 had no recent upload in 2026, and continued participation differed sharply by prior standing. Production also changed fundamentally. Median video duration fell from 247 to 60 seconds, with shortening across every content category and channel size. Among channels above 100,000 subscribers, new entrants accounted for most of the shift toward short form, while most continuing incumbents also shortened their output. Attention became more concentrated even among the same channels observed at both dates, and advertising revenue grew more slowly than the population meeting the subscriber threshold. These findings show how the output imperative extends from producing more to adapting what is produced, while sustained participation remains sharply unequal. They also place the increasingly Asian geography of the creator economy at the center of questions about platform labor, opportunity, and precarity.

title: Beyond the Joke: A Thematic Content Analysis of Russian-Linked Meme Pages Targeting Azerbaijan
abstract: As internet memes evolved from mere entertainment into a tool of digital propaganda, their role in modern warfare has become increasingly significant. This study examines their role in the case of Russian-linked information operations targeting the Azerbaijani audience on Facebook. While the existing literature on meme-based Russian propaganda focuses heavily on the United States and Ukraine, the South Caucasus, one of the important regions of Russia’s “near abroad” policy, remains overlooked. The research addresses this critical gap by analyzing how these strategies are adapted to Azerbaijan's specific cultural and political context. The study relies on qualitative, multimodal analysis and emergent coding of 78 memes from nine Russian-linked Facebook pages targeting Azerbaijan between January 2023 and December 2024. The analysis identifies four consistent themes (the negative othering of the West, the discrediting of Western leaders, the reframing of the Nagorno-Karabakh Conflict, and the promotion of Azerbaijani sovereignty) and various propaganda techniques that have already been revealed in existing studies. The research paper concludes that these pages conduct a systematic influence campaign that sophisticatedly blends pro-Russian narratives with culturally conservative and patriotic domestic sentiments to resonate with the local audience.

title: Did local authorities lose revenue following banning unhealthy food advertising?
abstract: UK local authorities are increasingly exploring restrictions for the advertising of unhealthy foods on their estates to promote healthier food environments. Concerns about effects on revenue can be a barrier to progress. In this study, we provide preliminary evidence that these policies did not negatively affect total advertising revenue across four local authorities in North West England. In some cases, we found that revenue increased post-implementation.

title: Product Market Reform and Enterprise Software Diffusion: Evidence from European Industries
abstract: This paper examines whether product-market reforms in upstream network sectors are associated with faster diffusion of enterprise software in downstream European industries. The analysis combines Eurostat data on Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) and Customer Relationship Management (CRM) adoption with OECD ETCR and REGIMPACT indicators for 24 economies and 13 industries over 2010–2021. Reform exposure is constructed using major annual regulatory declines and fixed 2010 US input-output weights, while the empirical specification includes country-by-interval, industry-by-interval and country-industry fixed effects. Industries more exposed to major reforms experience faster growth in the combined ERP-CRM adoption index. At the median nonzero reform exposure, the estimate corresponds to approximately 1.5 percentage points of additional adoption growth. The response is stronger for CRM, while ERP is smaller and less precisely estimated. Minor and moderate regulatory changes show no comparable relationship. The results remain similar across alternative samples, reform thresholds and controls for the initial stage of software diffusion. The findings connect upstream product-market reform to downstream diffusion of organizational technologies.

title: Conceptualizing Political Consumerism in the Attention Economy
authors: Christopher Starke, Claes de Vreese, Natali Helberger
abstract: Social media platforms increasingly become targets of politically and ethically motivated user protest, yet existing approaches do not sufficiently explain how deliberate platform use can operate as political participation. This conceptual paper extends the established concept of political consumerism to the attention economy, defining it as individuals’ market-oriented behaviors to punish or reward social media platforms on political or ethical grounds. It argues that three main factors constrain political consumerism on social media platforms: opaque value extraction, limited ethical alternatives, and high switching costs. Because political consumerism can take many forms, the paper suggests distinguishing user actions by their economic impact and whether they signal user preferences to the platform company. It further explains how social media literacy and regulation can improve the legibility and actionability of these practices. Finally, it outlines methodological implications for studying political consumerism through mixed-method designs that combine user motivations with behavioral data.

title: Resilience in a Discordant Security Culture: Georgia between Institutional Continuity and Political Realignment
abstract: Challenging the common understanding in the relevant literature, this study reconceptualizes resilience to hybrid threats as a politically mediated process rather than purely a matter of institutional capacity-building. To examine how policy frameworks and political rhetoric interact to shape resilience, it traces Georgia’s security culture in the aftermath of the Russo-Georgian war. Through intertextual discourse analysis, the article cross-examines the institutional architecture of digital resilience, encompassing cybersecurity (systemic), media regulation (protective) and media literacy (empowerment) measures, with the government’s shifting rhetoric (2023–2025), while interview data provide contextual insights. The analysis reveals a discordant security culture manifested in fragmented governance and discursive struggle over resilience. Although formal policy frameworks normatively align with the West and consistently identify Russia as the principal security threat, governmental rhetoric portrays the same Western actors as sources of foreign interference and prioritizes political autonomy over cooperation while still invoking commitments to the constitutionally enshrined Euro-Atlantic trajectory. This dichotomy between institutional design and political discourse results in strategic ambiguity. It suggests that in hybrid regimes formal frameworks may function symbolically to signal external alignment, while practice is determined by short-term political calculations and discretionary authority, leaving institutions and societies vulnerable to evolving forms of foreign interference.

title: From Desktop to Spatial Interfaces: UX Design Implications of Evolving Interaction Paradigms
abstract: This study examines how the transition from screen-based interaction paradigms to spatial interfaces affects established user experience principles and design considerations. The study is guided by the following research question: How does the transition from screen-based interaction paradigms to spatial interfaces affect established UX principles and design considerations? Apple Vision Pro and visionOS are examined as one case. The corpus consists of 60 selected Human Interface Guidelines pages, 76 WWDC sessions, the Apple Vision Pro User Guide, and notes from researcher observation. The HIG and WWDC materials were analyzed qualitatively and coded using four dimensions: consistency, feedback, affordance, and information architecture. The analysis suggests that established UX principles remain relevant in spatial interfaces, although the way they are implemented changes. This study describes that change through three categories: retention, adaptation, and extension. Some familiar purposes and structures remain in place, others are adapted through spatial interaction, and some design concerns expand to include the user’s body and surrounding environment. Familiar structures such as windows, controls, and navigation remain important, but visionOS adds gaze, gesture, depth, distance, sound, anchoring, and immersion as additional design mechanisms. From this pattern, the study proposes selective spatiality: spatial presentation, immersion, and embodied interaction are most useful when they support the task, not simply because they are available on the platform. In the Vision Pro case, effective spatial UX comes from keeping familiar interaction structures while adding spatial features only where they are useful. Designers must also consider comfort, attention, accessibility, environmental awareness, and hardware limits. Because the study examines one platform and does not include independent user testing, its findings should be interpreted within that scope.

title: Behavioural Sociology of Humans and Machines
authors: Taha Yasseri, Hao Cui, Nico Mutzner
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly participates in communication, decision-making, and collective action, making the social organisation of human–machine interaction central to Hybrid Intelligence (HI). This chapter reviews the behavioural sociology of humans and machines through an HI lens, examining how interaction and feedback shape the combination of human and artificial capabilities. Drawing on sociology, social psychology, human–computer interaction, organisational studies, collective intelligence, and science and technology studies, it traces processes from individual social perception to cooperation in hybrid groups and organisational and institutional arrangements. Particular attention is given to how machine participation alters familiar mechanisms: social categorisation attaches expectations to designed identities, reciprocity may involve unequal social obligations, and algorithmic recommendations acquire authority through organisational practices. The chapter distinguishes observable machine behaviour from human interpretations of intention, understanding, and moral responsibility. It also considers how behavioural effects can extend beyond direct human–machine encounters, while separating established findings from proposed longer-term consequences. It argues that the benefits of HI depend on how roles, incentives, reliance, and accountability are organised, and identifies priorities for empirical research on these evolving sociotechnical arrangements.

title: From Water Scarcity to Paceklik: Ecological Memory in Banyumas Literary and Expressive Traditions
abstract: Abstract Water is more than a physical necessity in communities whose everyday life has historically been closely connected with agriculture, seasonal rainfall, and the availability of water. It can become an object of desire, ritual expectation, narrative valuation, social celebration, and material anxiety. This article examines how such relationships are articulated across four Banyumasan literary and expressive traditions: Banyu Emas, Cowongan, Ricik-Ricik, and Ahmad Tohari’s Ronggeng Dukuh Paruk. The study employs qualitative comparative interpretation within an ecocritical framework and uses the concept of ecological memory in a deliberately bounded cultural sense. Rather than treating ecological memory as proof of a population’s psychological recollection of particular environmental events, the article defines it as the recurrent cultural articulation of human–environment relationships through forms in which environmental experience can be represented, performed, retained, and reinterpreted. The analysis finds that the four corpus units do not constitute a single environmental narrative or a continuous chain of cultural transmission. Their significance lies instead in the different ways cultural form transforms environmental experience. Banyu Emas renders water scarcity as a condition that gives water extraordinary value; Cowongan turns uncertainty over rainfall into ritual supplication and collective anticipation; Ricik-Ricik constructs the arrival of drizzle or rain as an occasion of happiness, humor, sociability, and play; while Ronggeng Dukuh Paruk connects drought with agricultural disruption, paceklik, food scarcity, and bodily vulnerability. The comparison extends ecological-memory discussion by demonstrating that environmental memory can encompass positive affect as well as crisis, including happiness, relief, humor, and anticipation. It also suggests that recurrence should not be confused with transmission and that continuity may occur through transformation rather than preservation. Ecological memory, in this formulation, persists because environmental relationships remain culturally productive even when the forms and meanings through which they are expressed change.

title: Enduring and Emerging Issues in Early Childhood Home Visiting: A Survey of Key Interest Groups
authors: Allison West, Lauren Klein, Kimberly Mihayo, Kay O'Neill, Jane Daniels, Jon Korfmacher
abstract: Background: Early childhood home visiting is a voluntary, two generation approach to promote the health and well-being of pregnant women and families with young children. The purpose of this survey was to assess enduring and emerging issues in home visiting within an evolving service delivery landscape. Methods: We recruited participants from a broad range of home visiting interest groups through an established practice-based research network. Participants completed a survey in which they selected the issues that were most concerning to them from a predetermined list and provided reasons for their selections as open text responses. We calculated the frequency with which each issue was endorsed and synthesized qualitative explanations for the top third of all issues selected. Results: The issues endorsed most frequently were supporting families when community resources aren’t available, funding stability, family recruitment and engagement, workforce well-being and retention, and administrative burden. Conclusions: Survey results highlight the strong influence of community context and funding on home visiting implementation and outcomes, enduring questions regarding family recruitment and engagement, and opportunities to support and strengthen the workforce. Findings will inform collaborative, applied research to identify gaps, develop solutions, and advance home visiting policy and practice.

title: How does the level of media propaganda literacy differ among individuals under 18, between 18 and 30, and over 30 in Uzbekistan, and how does this difference impact their vulnerability to misinformation and critical thinking skills?
abstract: This research investigates how varying levels of media propaganda literacy across different age groups in Uzbekistan impact susceptibility to misinformation and critical thinking. By categorizing participants into three distinct age groups—those under 18, between 18 and 30, and over 30—the study identifies generational differences shaped by historical and technological contexts. Data collected through surveys and interviews reveal that while younger generations rely more on social media and demonstrate greater adaptability to digital information, older individuals remain dependent on traditional media like television, often lacking critical fact-checking skills. Despite a high level of self-reported understanding of concepts like "propaganda," significant knowledge gaps persist, particularly among older participants, highlighting the enduring impact of Soviet-era media practices. The findings underscore the need for targeted media literacy initiatives tailored to age-specific vulnerabilities to bridge generational divides and empower all citizens to evaluate information critically

title: An Integrated Multi-Method Approach to Television Studies in the Streaming Era: the Production, Representation, and Reception of Gender Violence on Norwegian Screens
abstract: By merging textual analysis with production interviews and audience studies, this article aims to develop a multi-method approach to television texts. The method proves particularly useful to investigate audiences’ interpretation of gender violence on screen and how this is integrated within a Public Service Broadcaster’s societal mission and national audiences’ perception of the broadcaster. The article focuses on the most popular Norwegian TV series to date Exit (2019-2023) distributed by the national NRK, as a product of enlightening entertainment. It questions how aesthetic choices create realism and how different audiences relate to the reality presented as authentic and relatable. It also interrogates how audiences’ perception of the national broadcaster affect their interpretation of the series.

title: Pretender: When Organizations Perform Competence Instead of Creating Value
abstract: This paper develops the concept of Pretender to explain a condition in which organizations increasingly prioritize demonstrating that they function properly over producing the substantive value those functions are meant to create. The idea originated from an everyday Japanese expression, gokko (ごっこ), loosely meaning “playing at” a role or activity. Here, gokko does not imply deliberate deception, incompetence, or conscious fakery. Rather, it points to situations in which management, expertise, reflection, adjudication, or organizational response becomes partially detached from its substantive function while retaining value as evidence that the function exists.
